OBITUARY REFERENCES
MR. CHAIRMAN: Honourable Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing
away of Shri Sudhir Ranjan Mazumdar, a former Member of this House on the 4th of
January, 2009 at the age of 69 years.
Born at Gangra village in the Comilla District of Bangladesh in May 1939, Shri Mazumdar
had his education at M.G .M.H.S. School, Maharaj Bir Bikram College and Calcutta University.
A teacher and a social worker, Shri Mazumdar organised and participated in various
social service programmes during natural calamities, particularly in Bangladesh, during
the Indo-Pak War of 1970-71. He started his legislative career with the membership of the
Tripura Legislative Assembly, where he was a Member from 10.1.1983 to 5.2.1988, 5.2.1988
to 18.2.1992 and, again, from 14.3.2008 to 4.1.2009. At the time of his death, he was a sitting
Member of the Tripura Legislative Assembly. Shri Mazumdar served as the Chief Minister
of Tripura from 5.2.1988 to 18.2.1992, during that period, he took welfare measures and
promoted good governance in the State. Earlier, he had also served as the Leader of the
Opposition in the Tripura Legislative Assembly.
Shri Sudhir Ranjan Mazumdar represented the State of Tripura in this House from
April, 1992 to April, 1998.
In the passing away of Shri Sudhir Ranjan Mazumdar, the country has lost a
distinguished social worker, an able parliamentarian and an administrator.
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Sudhir Ranjan Mazumdar.
I request the Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of respect
to the memory of the departed.
[Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute]
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary General will convey to the members of the bereaved
family our sense of profound sorrow and deep sympathy.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Satyam Computers Scam
*21. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister of CORPORATE AFFAIRS
be pleased to state:
(a) whether any significant headway has been made into the Satyam Computers
Scam;
(b) if so, the details thereof, indicating the extent of misappropriation of funds, the
period for which these irregularities have been going on;
(c) the extent of involvement of auditors and others in the Scam; and

[RAJYA SABHA]2
(d) the steps taken/proposed to be taken to ensure to detect other cases of profit
boosting and other corporate frauds?
THE MINISTER OF CORPORATE AFFAIRS (SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA): (a) to (d):
A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.
Statement
(a) to (c) The Government has ordered investigation on 13.1.2009 under Sec. 235 of the
Companies Act, 1956 into the affairs of M/s Satyam Computer Services Ltd. to be carried
out by Inspectors drawn from the office of Serious Fraud Investigation Office. In addition,
the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India is also examining the role and the conduct
of the statutory auditors of the Company with regard to the statutory functions required
to be discharged by them. The said investigations and enquiries are currently under
progress.
(d) Under the framework provided by the Companies Act, 1956, all companies are
required to make statutory disclosures that reflect true and fair view of the state of affairs
of the company. To facilitate making of such disclosures by companies and for easy
viewing of the same by the stakeholders of the companies, general public and regulatory
agencies, Government has set up an electronic registry with round - the - clock access
through internet. Legal action is taken against such companies that do not comply with
the requirement. In addition, the Act provides for appointment of independent, statutory
auditors to audit the accounts and report to the shareholders. Such audited accounts are
also displayed on the electronic registry for general viewing. While the reporting
requirements are regulated under the Companies Act, 1956, the conduct of auditors is
regulated under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. In addition, for listed companies,
compliance with these statutory requirements is required to be certified by a company
secretary in practice, who in turn is regulated under the Company Secretaries Act, 1980.
The Act also provides powers to the Government to undertake inspection/ investigation
of companies and for prosecution for false statements relating to the Company in the
prospectus, the financial statements or otherwise. Subject to approvals by Company Law
Board, the Government can also take action against mismanagement and oppression in
companies by effecting changes in the management of the companies. Companies as are
listed on stock exchanges are also subject to regulation by Securities and Exchange Board
of India (SEBI) Act, 1992. The Government and various regulatory agencies take appropriate
action under the Companies Act, 1956 and other laws, as warranted, to detect and deal
with cases of falsehoods or corporate fraud, as the case may be, through the application
of the existing statutory framework.

finance companies or banking companies, they have to approach the Reserve Bank of

statutory auditors. The Reserve Bank of India has no legal power to blacklist any audit
firm. That is the job of the Institute of Chartered Accountants, and in fact, they also
cannot blacklist. They can issue an advisory. The Reserve Bank of India can issue an
advisory that the auditors of this firm, the partners of this firm have been found guilty of
some misconduct, and therefore, this company or this firm may not be engaged for the
audit work of a particular bank or a ccompany. So, this is the situation. With regard to the
accounts of the Global Trust Bank for 2002-03, certain deficiencies were noticed, and
therefore, the Reserve Bank of India had issued some sort of an advisory to banks and
NBFCs in October 2004 not to engage the Pricewaterhouse. After 3 years, that is, in
August 2007, Pricewaterhouse approached the Reserve Bank of India to consider allowing
them to carry on with the auditor work, and that is how the RBI, in their wisdom, thought
that this punishment of 3 years is good enough and they lifted the ban.

Establishment of museums at district and regional level
*22. MS. MABEL REBELLO:
SHRI B. J. PANDA:
Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is proposed to establish more museums at district and regional levels
to take the museum movement to the people in the country;
Written Answers to Starred Questions

[RAJYA SABHA]18
(b) if so, the details thereof;
(c) whether it is also proposed to redefine the museum concept to keep pace with the
evolving social changes;
(d) if so, the details thereof; and
(e) what are the details of districts/regions where this new concept is proposed to be
implemented in Orissa and Jharkhand?
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI): (a) to (d) In order to
strengthen the museum movement and to re-invigorate the existing museum scenario in
the country the scheme for financial assistance for "Promotion and Strengthening of
Regional and Local Museums" was revised by Government in September, 2008. The salient
features of the revised scheme are as under:-
i. Financial assistance upto Rs. 6 crores for setting up of a Museum under Category-I
(State Museums and other Museums with exquisite collections) and upto Rs. 3 crores
for setting up a Museums under Category-II (Regional and Local Museums).
ii. Financial Assistance to existing museums for upgradation and modernization was
enhanced from Rs. 1.70 Crore to Rs. 5.00 crores in respect of Category-I Museums and
from Rs. 60.00 lakhs to Rs. 2.5 crores in respect of Category-II Museums.
iii. The scheme envisages financing by Government of India upto 80% of the estimated
amount (90% in case of museums in NE regions)
iv. Training and refresher courses for the museum staff are included as an integral part of
the Scheme.
v. Purchase of exhibits is not financed under the Scheme.
(e) The scheme is applicable to all eligible museums from all States, including Orissa
and Jharkhand.
Transportation of oil from caspian region
*23. SHRIMATI VIPLOVE THAKUR: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state:
(a) whether the issue of transportation of oil from Caspian region through the
Mediterranean and Red Sea into India was discussed during the visit of Foreign Minister
of Turkey to India in February, 2008;
(b) if so, the salient features of the discussion;
(c) whether it is also a fact that oil, if brought from Caspian region through the
Mediterranean and Red Sea, will be cheaper;
(d) if so, whether Government has taken any decision on the issue; and
(e) if so, the details thereof?
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MURLI DEORA): (a)
and (b) The Foreign Minister of Turkey, during his visit to India in February 2008, had
Written Answers to Starred Questions

[17 FEBRUARY , 2009] 19
outlined a proposal for cooperation between Turkey, Israel and India for transportation of
crude oil from the Caspian region through the Mediterranean and Red Sea and into India.
Briefly, this project envisages transport of crude oil from Ceyhan port in Turkey to Ashkelon
port in Israel in the Mediterranean Sea, initially through Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs)
and eventually by laying a sub-sea pipeline. Thereafter, crude oil will be transported
through the existing Ashkelon -Eilat pipeline in Israel to Eilat port on the Red Sea. From
there, crude oil may be carried to India/other parts of Asia. The project is still in a conceptual
stage and requires a detailed feasibility study to establish its techno-commercial viability.
A tripartite meeting between Turkey-Israel-India was held in September 2008 at Ankara to
discuss conceptual features of the project.

(b) whether oil demand declined by 47 trillion barrel per day (tb/d) in October, 2008
following the highest figure of plus 200 tb/d of the year in September, 2008;

Black marketing of LPG cylinders in Delhi
179. MS. MABEL REBELLO:
SHRI B.J. PANDA:
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL/GAS be pleased to state:

(b) whether some raids were conducted by Government to assess the enormity of
this menace; and
Written Answers to Unstarred Questions

[17 FEBRUARY , 2009] 87
(c) if so, the details thereof, inter-alia indicating the action plan of Government to
effectively control this menace?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL
GAS (SHRI DINSHA PATEL): (a) to (c) The possibility of blackmarketing/ diversion of
subsidized domestic LPG cylinders by some unscrupulous elements cannot be ruled out
due to the wide gap between the retail price of LPG for domestic use and the market price
for commercial LPG.
OMCs have detected 16 cases of diversion of LPG by their LPG distributorship in the
NCT of Delhi during the period April, 2008 to December, 2008. Action against the erring
distributors was taken as per provisions of Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG)/
Distributorship Agreement.
In order to stop blackmarketing/ diversion of domestic LPG cylinders, the Government
has enacted "Liquefied Petroleum Gas (Regulation of Supply and Distribution) Order,
2000" and formulated "Marketing Discipline Guidelines, 2001" which provides for penal
action against LPG distributors indulging in diversion/ blackmarketing of LPG .
Whenever OMCs receive complaints, these are investigated and if the /complaint is
established, suitable action is taken against the LPG distributor(s) in /accordance with the
provisions of the Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG). MDG provides for following
action against the distributor:-
– Fine of Rs. 20,000 plus the price of LPG diverted at commercial rates for 1st offence.
– Fine of Rs. 50,000 plus the price of LPG diverted at commercial rates for 2nd offence.
– Termination of the distributorship for 3rd offence.
In addition to the action taken by the OMCs, State Governments are empowered under
the LPG (Regulation of Supply & Distribution) Order, 2000 promulgated under the Essential
Commodities Act, 1955 to take action against blackmarketing/diversion of domestic LPG .
Similarly, the Weights and Measures Departments of the States / UTs initiate legal action
against those LPG distributors found blackmarketing/diversion of LPG cylinders. The
State Governments have been alerted from time to time to take steps against the
biackmarketing/diversion of domestic cylinders for unauthorized usage.
Government have issued advertisements cautioning the public that use of domestic
LPG for non-domestic purposes is illegal, dangerous and against national interest. Through
these advertisements, cooperation of the general public has also been sought to report
any irregularity / malpractice to the OMCs.
The officials of OMCs carry out random checks at distributors godowns, delivery
points, as well as en-route to ensure that no misuse takes place. The distributors of OMCs
are under strict instructions to check the weight of cylinders at their godowns before
delivery, and only cylinders with the specified weight are to be delivered to the customers.
The distributors have also been instructed to ensure that the seals are verified & shown
to the customers at the time of delivery. In case any under-weight cylinder is received by
the customer, such cylinders are replaced free of charge by the OMCs.
OMCs have introduced different colours for domestic and non-domestic LPG cylinders
for controlling the diversion of domestic LPG for unauthorized use.

Technology upgradation of refineries
†190.SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA:
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI:
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is a fact that on an average 28 to 29 litres of petrol and 85 litres of diesel
are yielded by processing of one barrel of crude oil in crude oil processing industries of
the country;
(b) if not, the details thereof and the average production of petrol and diesel from
processing of one barrel of crude oil in oil refineries of the country;
(c) whether this average can be increased by technology upgradation; and
(d) if so, the reaction of Government in this regard?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL
GAS (SHRI DINSHA PATEL): (a) and (b) The average production of petrol and diesel in
India varies from refinery to refinery depending upon the configuration and type of crude
oil processed. Most of the inland refineries in India were established based on low sulphur
indigenous crude oil processing whereas the coastal refineries predominantly process
high sulphur imported crude oil. The average yield in the country is only 17 litres of petrol
and 65 litres of diesel.
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The average yield can be increased to certain extent through
selective crude oil processing and substantially through improved secondary processing,
i.e. technology upgradation and improved configuration. The oil Public Sector Undertakings
have continuously implemented projects to increase refining capacity and maximization of
distillates in order to achieve self-sufficiency in petroleum products in the country. Fluidized
Catalytic Cracking, Hydrocracking, Hydrotreaters, Delayed Cokers, Catalytic Reformers,
Isomerization, Alkylation Units etc. have been selectively added in the refineries for
maximization of distillate yield including petrol and diesel.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL

and Island territories) and optional blending of 10% ethanol with petrol from October 2007

pilot projects have been undertaken at two locations at Aonla Depot in U.P. and  Desur
Depot in Karnataka from 15.12.2008 and 20.12.2008 respectively. The pilot study is likely to
be completed by 30.6.2009.

Fixation of sale price of petrol and diesel
†209.SHRI RAM JETHMALANI:
SHRI SHIV ANAND TIWARI:
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is a fact that the rate of consumer sale prices of petrol and diesel in the
country is fixed on the basis of trade parity pricing system;
(b) if so, the details of expenditure regarding the product being factored under the
above system;
(c) the reasons for adaptation of above system instead of common basis of production
cost to fix the consumer sale price; and
(d) the differences and characteristics of above said both systems?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL
GAS (SHRI DINSHA PA TEL): (a) and (b) Based on the Rangarajan Committee's
recommendations, effective 16 June 2006, Government approved the refinery gate pricing
of Petrol and Diesel on Trade Parity basis, which is the weighted average of Import Parity
and Export Parity prices, in the ratio of 80:20. The build up of retail selling price of Petrol
and Diesel includes the following elements:
(i) Price paid to refinery on Trade Parity basis.
(ii) Inland freight up to the market
(iii) Marketing Margin
(iv) Dealer Commission
(v) Excise duty
(vi) V alue Added tax and local levies
(c) and (d) As the country imports more than 75% of its crude oil requirements, domestic
prices of petroleum products are, to a very large extent, influenced by international oil
prices. Hence, the adoption of Trade Parity pricing for Petrol and Diesel. In petroleum
refining, crude oil is processed through numerous processing streams. The blending of
intermediate product streams from various processing units for making finished petroleum
products makes its difficult to apportion the total cost to individual refined products with
reasonable accuracy. Therefore, individual product-wise costs are not identified separately.
The Government dismantled Administered Pricing Mechanism (APM) w.e.f. 1st April,
2002, which was based on the cost plus methodology for determining prices of petroleum
products. The APM had the following disadvantages:
(1) APM: did not provide strong incentives for investments in technological upgradations
or for cost minimization.

(2) There was no incentive for oil companies to generate internal resources for making
investments for the future.
(3) Private capital as well as foreign direct investment would not be forthcoming in view
of the regulatory controls inherent in the APM.
(4) Subsidies and cross-subsidies resulted in wide distortions in the consumer prices
and did not reflect the economic cost of petroleum products.
The Government's decision to determine domestic prices of petroleum products on the
basis of international prices is intended to make the oil companies globally competitive, to
attract investments in petroleum sector to meet the growing demand, and to promote
efficiency and better customer service through competition.

Water Requirement of increasing population
241. SHRI MOHD. ALI KHAN: Will the Minister of W ATER RESOURCES be pleased
to state:
(a) whether population of the country is expected to 140 crore by 2025; and
(b) if so, the steps being taken to give water to each State to meet the population
requirements in each State especially in Andhra Pradesh?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF W ATER RESOURCES (SHRI JAI
PRAKASH NARAYAN YADA V): (a) As per report of Technical Group on Population
Projection constituted by National Commission on Population, the projection of the
population of country is 139 crore by 2025.
(b) Various steps for planning and implementation of water resources projects for
meeting the projected requirement of water for different purposes are taken by the
respective State Governments. Government of Andhra Pradesh have informed that several
activities related to development of water resources have been taken up under
"Jalayagnam".
Ministry of Water Resources provides central assistance under its various programmes
to all States including Andhra Pradesh. Due emphasis has been laid on development and
management of water resources projects during the XI Plan. An outlay of Rs. 2,32,311
crore has been provided for the irrigation, command area development  and  water
management and flood control in the XI Plan against the X Plan outlay of Rs.95,743 crore.

Dismay over Disinvestment of PSU  Shares
SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN (West Bengal) : Sir, I rise to express my concern
over the renewed move of the Government to start disinvestment in the profitable
public sector. Only one day before, in Lok Sabha, and also in this House, while
commending the Budget, the hon. Finance Minister spoke quite high of the role of
the public sector in stabilising and protecting the national economy, in the background
of the severe global financial crisis. But, immediately after that commendment made in
Budget, on the next day, as reported by the Press, the Government is again planning
to offload shares of the profitable public sector in the market. That is totally against
the national interest and particularly so, when the stock market is sinking.
The prices are going down, and at this time, this renewed initiative to sell out
the shares of the profitable public sector means handing over the control of the public

sector units to private hands at throw away prices because now the prices are sinking,
and this is all the more dangerous particularly when the public sector companies are
also having different other routes to raise money through bonds and debentures, and
in the changed financial circumstances, common people are having more faith on the
bonds and debentures issued by the public sector. So, it is not just necessary that
the equity route has to be adopted by the public sector to raise funds. So, from all
logic, this is completely illogical proposition to go in for offloading shares of the public
sector, and through you, Sir, I urge upon the Government not to resort to such a
dangerous exercise which will finally mean a total fraud of a different type on the
national economy and the people of the country.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER
Regarding Alleged Misbehaviour of Police in Jharkhand
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM) : This morning,
hon. Member Shri Yashwant Sinha and certain other hon. Members made submissions
on the incidents that took place at the gates of the Raj Bhawan in Ranchi, Jharkhand
on February 12, 2009. I have been briefed on the submissions and I am distressed
that such an incidents should have taken place on that day.
The Government of India has received information from the State Government. The
DGP, Jharkhand has also report.
It is reported that prominent leaders of the BJP, along with a few thousands
workers, marched towards the several gates of the Raj Bhawan. At gate no. 3, the
demonstrators were led by two MLAs; they demonstrated peacefully behind the
barricade; and there was no incident. At gate no. 4 the demonstrators were ley by an
MLA; they also demonstrated peacefully behind the barricade and there was on
incident.
The incident occurred between gate no. 2 and no.1 which is the main gate. It is
reported that the demonstrators were led by Shri Yashwant Sinha, M.P., Shri Arjun
Munda, MLA, Shri Saryu Rai, MLA, Shri Dinesh Sarangi, MLA, Shri Loknath Mahto,
Statement by Minister

[RAJYA SABHA]212
MLA and Shri Raghubar Das, MLA and States President, BJP. Announcements were
made over the public address system that orders under Section 144, Cr. P.C. had been
promulgated in that area. Notwithstanding the announcement, the demonstrators broke
the barricade and moved towards gate no. 2. Thereafter, ignoring repeated
announcements over the public address system that the assembly had become unlawful
and that the demonstrators should disperse, the demonstrators broke the second
barricade outside gate no. 2 nad proceeded towards gate no. 1.
In roder to contain the agitators, the police used a water cannon. When that failed
to deter the agitators, the police had no option but to resort to a mild lathi charge.
According to the report submitted by the Director-General of Police, Shri Yashwant
Sinha, Shri Arjun Munda and Shri Saryu Rai, besides some others, sustained injuries.
I have with me the injury reports, but since Shri Yashwant Sinha himself has stated
before the House that he was not complaining about the injuries, it may not be
necessary to refer to the injury reports. However, I may add that the Circle Officer,
Namkum, Shri Amit Kumar personally accompanied Shri Yashwant Sinha to the Seva
Sadan Hospital where he was treated. Shri Arjun Munda and Shri Saryu Rai were taken
by the officers of the District Administration to Adre House, where the doctors
attached to Raj Bhawan administered first aid to them. Shri Yashwant Sinha and the
two MLAs were arrested at about 1430 hours and were released at about Shri
Yashwant Sinha has referred to certain persons who were injured. We have gathered
the facts. The DGP, Jharkhand has reported that Shri Ram Jatan Paswan, PSO, suffered
an abrasion on te left knee which was a simple injury. A police constable by name
Shri Prakash Kumar suffered a lacerated wound on the left side of the scalp, which
was also a simple injury. We have not been able to gather any information about the
injuries to Shri Himanshu, Private Secretary to Shri Yashwant Sinha, since the police
have not been able to locate ay injury report in that case. If Shri Yashwant Sinha
would be kind enough to share with me more information about the hospital or doctor
who treated Shri Himanshu, I shall endeavour to gather more information.
According to the records the Nagarmal Modi Seva Sadan Hospital, 89
demonstrators were registered as patients, out of which two had suffered fractures on
the leg and one had suffered a head injury. They were admitted to the hospital and
subsequently discharged. The district administration has reported that 15 police
personnel also sustained minor injuries due to stone pelting and use of sticks by the
demonstrators.
DGP, Jharkhand has reported that 300 demonstrators were detained adn released
later in the evening.
DGP, Jharkhand has also reported that the district administration had, by a fax
message, informed the Secretary General, Rajya Sabha and the Speaker of the State
Legislative Assembly without any delay on the same evening, that is, February 12,
2009 about the arrest and release of the Members of the respective Houses. However,
on being advised that the message in respect of Shri Yashwant Sinha should have
been addressed to the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, another fax message was sent
on February 13, 2009 to the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha.
Statement by Minister

[17 FEBRUARY , 2009] 213
Mr. Vice-Chairman, I am distressed and unhappy that such an incident should have
taken place. I have placed the facts before the House. I have great respect for hon.
Members who have complained about the alleged police excess, but I am not able to
make any judgement in this behalf. I offer my sympathies to those who have suffered
injuries. I wish that such demonstrations are conducted peacefully and no cause is
given for any action by the police.

me an opportunity to place our views on the Motion of Thanks on the President's Address.
The President's Address is a compliation of the functioning of the UPA Government
during the last five years. It is nothing but a jugglery of statistics and date collection. Sir,
I would like to focus on there major issues with reference to this President's Address,
namely, the Sri Lankan Tamil issue, the functioning of the telecommunications and the
spectrum scandal and the UPA Government's handling of terrorism during its tenure.
Sir, the plight of innocent Tamil civilians of Sri Lanka is a serious concern. The on-
going war between the Government of Sri Lanka and the LTTE has resulted in a humanitarian
disaster, including massive civilian casualties and the internal displacemtn of nearly 250,000
innocent civilians. Under the guise of war, the Sir Lankan Government  has been creating
a humanitarian crisis of a gargantuan proportion by systematically cleansing the Tamil
ethnicity. It is a clear genocide of Tamils. Lakhs of Tamil people in Mullaitheevu are
suffering without any food or medicine, facing annihilation due to indiscirminate shelling

Clearances to FDI proposals 
 *41. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 
be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Finance Ministry has given its clearance to 32 FDI proposals worth Rs. 846 
crores; 
 (b) if so, whether a decision of 3 media companies proposal has been deferred; and 
 (c) if so, what are other proposals pending with Government and by what time all 
proposals of FDI will be cleared and to what extent it will help to meet financial crisis? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRIAL POLICY AND 
PROMOTION, MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR): (a) to 
(c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
 (a) Yes, Sir. The Government of India approv ed 32 proposals of Foreign Direct Investment 
(FDI) amounting to approximately Rs. 845.7 cr ores based on the recommendations of Foreign 
Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) in its meeting held on November 18, 2008. 
 (b) Yes, Sir. The proposals of (i) M/s. Lokmat Newspapers Pvt. Ltd., Mumbai; (ii) M/s 
Prithvi Prakashan Pvt. Ltd., Mumbai; and (iii) M/s Dow Jones and Company Inc., USA were 
deferred in the meeting of FIPB on November 18, 2008. Subsequently M/s Lokmat Newspapers 
Pvt. Ltd., and M/s Prithvi Prakashan Pvt. Ltd., withdrew their proposals. The proposal of M/s 
Dow Jones and Company Inc., USA has been appr oved by the Foreign Investment Promotion 
Board (FIPB) in its meeting held on 9-1-2009. 
 (c) Up to 31-1-2009, there are 49 proposals with the FIPB where requisite information 
from the concerned Ministries of the respective company has to be received. 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Sir, the reply gi ven by the hon. Minister does not answer 
all the questions that I have raised. Part (c) of my question was, to what extent the proposals 
would help meet the financial crisis. That has no t been replied to. How much time it would take 
to clear the proposals has also not been said. Furthermore, I would like to ask the hon. Minister, 
through you, Sir, how much has the FDI shortfall been this year due to the global financial crisis 
and what is the Government trying to do to over come this and attract more funds flow into the 
country? 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Is that one question or two? 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Sir, it is one question, relating to FDI. What is the 
Government trying to do to attr act more funds flow into the country, particularly into the area of 
industries where more employment is generated, and the core industry? 

 5
 SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, the question asked by the hon. Member has been answered 
in full. He has asked to what extent FDI would ease out the pressure of the economic situation. 
We have said that as on 31st January, 49 prop osals are still pending with FIPB for want of 
requisite information. As and when the informat ion is received, these would be taken up and 
depending upon to what the extent or nature of the proposals are, what is the value and volume 
of investment that is to come in, we will take a view on that. 
Sir, the other question that wa s asked was what are we doing to attract FDI in the country. 
It is a much larger question and I have no difficulty in answering that. All the steps that have been 
taken so far are intended to make India as an investment-friendly destination and a series of 
measures have been taken. Despite the global economic slowdown, we are happy to inform the 
hon. House that India still hopes to go by about 7 per cent in GDP terms in 2008-09. So, I think 
that there is the reality of a global economic slowdown. But the FDI constitutes a very small 
fraction in what we need to do. But even so, ou r attempt or endeavour is to make India as an 
investment-friendly destination. 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Sir, the FDI which has already come into the country has 
been getting withdrawn time and again because of the meltdown all over the world. Is there any 
proposal or new scheme or new incentive that the Government is proposing to see that whatever 
FDI comes into the country gets retained and re-invested in the country? 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, I am happy to inform the House that when this Government 
came to office in 2004 the investment in terms of FDI was about 2.5 billion dollars. This year, 
despite the global economic slowdown, we hope to receive about 30 billion dollars in terms of 
FDI. Despite all that is happening in the world, India still offers the best destination in terms of 
return on FDI. This is an economy that is still gr owing at about 7 per cent per annum; this is still 
an economy where it is widely perceived that we have reasonable rates of return on investment 
and that has been possible because of a series of calibrated measures that have been taken in 
the last four years to liberalise the FDI regime. There is no restriction on manufacturing. Even 100 
per cent FDI can be brought into manufacturing ex cept for seven or eight stated exceptions. In 
addition to that, in a whole range of sectors in the economic spheres, we have increased the FDI 
caps and raised them to 49 per cent to 51 per cent to 74 per cent depending upon the sensitivity 
of the sectors involved. So, on the whole, the Government has done exceedingly well on this 
front, and I would like to assure the hon. Member and other hon. Members of the House that on 
this score India continues to be the most favour able investment destination. Sir, A.T. Kearney 
has stated that, UNCTAD Report has stated that, McKinsey Report has stated that and all the 
reports of international standards have confirmed that India continues to be a favourable 
investment destination.

SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: I would like to put my question through you to the hon. Minister. Is 
it a fact that the Government has taken a step in  libralising Foreign Direct Investment Guidelines 
recently and the sectoral cap on FDI has been nullified by excluding investment by companies 
owned or controlled by Indians having substantial foreign capital? By this redefinition, if it has 
happened, FDI can be routed through Indian companies..(Interruptions).. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please ask the question. 
SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: Indian companies are not to be classified as FDI. My question is: If 
it is so, why is the Government bypassing this Pa rliament? Is it not a fact that the Government 
has taken a decision by a backdoor policy to remove that cap on FDI in different sectors? 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, the policy on FDI is constantly in a state of review from time to 
time. We take a measured view on what is require d to be done in the light of the experiences of 
the past. I would, at the threshold, like to allay the apprehensions of the hon. Member that there 
is no question of any backdoor dilution of the sectoral caps. The only thing, that has been 
introduced in Press Note-2 of 2009, is that we have categorically and consciously taken a view, 
and we have so stated, that investments by a domestic company defined under the Indian 
Companies Act to mean where Indian residents own more than 51 per cent in terms of ownership 
and control shall not be treated as investment by foreign companies... 
SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: This is the backdoor policy. 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: I am answering. ...irrespective of whether a small percentage of 
foreign equity is in the Indian company, and I will tell learned hon. Member the reason for that. 
The reason is that what had happened in the past was that domestic companies were foreclosed 
from participating in mega investment projects  on this ground. So, we took a view that 
underlying purpose of sectoral caps was that in certain sectors, the control of the company must 
always remain in Indian hands. We have assure d that the control of the companies will always 
remain in Indian hands because 51 per cent Indian ownership leads to control being in Indian 
hands in terms of right to appoint Directors and to ensure the management of the company 
remains in Indian hands. So, the substance, spirit and letter of policy have been preserved. We 
have only ensured that domestic companies are not unreasonably foreclosed from participating 
in the economic activities in the country. 
DR. K. MALAISAMY: Sir, the hon. Minister seems to be well informed. Can I ask a free 
frank opinion of the hon. Minister? 

 7
 MR. CHAIRMAN: Opinion in the House is free and frank. 
DR. K. MALAISAMY: The global meltdown has do ne enough damage not only to the global 
economy but also to the Indian economy. In such a situation, I am inclined to ask whether the 
impact or effect of the global meltdown in Indi an economy is substantial or marginal. Whatever 
may be, can you give an assurance that our Indian economy will not be affected; if at all, that will 
be only marginal? 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, although this does not arise from the question, yet I have no 
hesitation in giving an honest answer to the ho n. Member’s question. Sir, in a global economy, 
for any country to say that its economy is to tally insulated from what happens abroad, is 
fallacious; it is wrong. I have no hesitation in  accepting, as has been  done by hon. Finance 
Minister, and earlier by Mr. Chidambaram, that we are not totally insulated. We are impacted by 
global economic slowdown, but thankfully for us, since the Indian economy is essentially driven 
by domestic consumption and demand, we are re latively less negatively impacted by global 
economic slowdown, and that is proved by the fa ct that whereas there is contraction in the 
economies of developed countries, India will still register a handsome growth of about 7 per 
cent. Therefore, I would like to assure hon. Member that we are less negatively impacted and we 
are responding as purposively and with utmost ex pedition as possible to respond to the global 
economic slowdown.

culture, society or politics of our country.

Implementation of Building and Other Construction Workers’ Act 
 †*42. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: †† 
  SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
 Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of 
Employment and Conditions of Services) Act, 1996 had been implemented in the country about 
12 years back; 
 (b) if not, the date of impl ementation of aforesaid law; 
 (c) whether State Governments had been empowered to collect cess for the welfare of 
workers under this Act; 
 (d) if so, the State-wise amount collected under this head till March, 2008; and 
 (e) the names of States where this collection was done and the names of schemes 
formulated out of this amount for welfare of workers? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINIST RY OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI 
OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
 (a) to (e) The Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and 
Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 and Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Cess 
Act, 1996 were enacted in 1996 and Central Rule s for these Acts were framed in 1998. The 
Central Government is the implementing authority for the establishments coming under central 
sphere while the State Governments are the impl ementing authority in the State sphere. The 
States have to frame and Notify Rules, cons titute Advisory Committees/Expert Committees, 
appoint various authorities for registration of wo rkers, Cess collection, Inspection and Appealing 
Authority and to constitute State Welfare Boards to frame and implement various welfare 
schemes in pursuance of the said Act. The States are at various stages of implementation of the 
two Acts. 
 State Governments are empowered to collect ce ss for the welfare of workers. Statements 
on the basis of information received from the State/UT Governments indicating the amount 
collected and welfare schemes formulated as on 31st March, 2008 are annexed as statement-I 
and II.

to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
 (a) The number of households which had demanded and were provided employment 
under NREGA during 2006-07 was 21188894 and 21016099 respectively and during 2007-08 was 
34287442 and 33889122 respectively. The number of households which has demanded and have 
been provided employment during 2008-09 (up to January, 2009) is 38077719 and 36968502 
respectively. State-wise details are given in the Statement-I (See below). 
 (b) 2142718 households were provided 100 days of employment during 2006-07, 3601926 
households were provided 100 days of employment during 2007-08 and 2713053 households 
have been provided 100 days of employment  during 2008-09 (upto January, 2009). State-wise 
details are given in Statement-II (See below). 
 (c) Average number of days of employment provided to each household in the year 2006-
07 was 43 days; in 2007-08 was 42 days and during 2008-09 (upto January-08) the average is 
41 days per household. State-wise details are given in Statement-III. (See below). 
 (d) Yes, Sir. NREGA is moving towards the fu lfillment of its objectives of augmentation of 
employment opportunities and creation of durable assets. Persondays generation under NREGA 
has increased in comparison with earlier wage employment programme of SGRY. Under SGRY 
an average of 81 crore person days were generated in a year in the entire country; whereas 
under NREGA, 90.5 crore person days were generated in 200 districts in 2006-07, 143.59 crore 
persondays were generated in 330 districts in  2007-08 and 152.14 crore person days have been 
generated in the entire country up to mid-January, 2009 reflecting an 88% increase over the 
previous wage employment programme. A sign ificant share in the employment generated 
belongs to SCs (30%). STs (25%) and women (49%). 20 lakh works have been taken up in 
the current financial year of which 46% relate to  water conservation, 18% to rural connectivity 
and 15% to land development. Individual land  owned by 4.30 lakh households belonging to 
SC/ST, BPL and IAY have been benefited from NR EGA works such as irrigation facility, land 
development and plantation. 
 Under the Act, employment is provided to a wage seeker for the number of days of 
employment demanded subject to an over all ce iling of 100 days per household in a financial

Issue of MNIC to check Bangladeshi infiltrators 
 *51. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
  SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
 Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether the Supreme Court has recently directed the Union Government to take 
immediate steps for issue of Multipurpose Nation al Identity Cards (MNIC) in the country to 
check the infiltration of Bangladeshis; 
 (b) if so, whether the Bangladeshis staying illegally in the country are having Ration 
Cards, Voter Cards, PAN Cards etc.; and 
 (c) if so, what initiatives would be taken to  ensure cent per cent exodus of Bangladeshis 
from the country? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS  
(DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) Yes Sir. The Supreme Court has made an observation to this 
effect in WP (Civil) No.125 of 1998. However, the Government has already decided  that a 
National Population Register (NPR) would be prepared for which details on specified 
characteristics shall be collected in respect of e ach individual who is a usual residents, at the 
time of next decennial Census in 2011. This in formation will include the photographs and finger 
biometrics of all those who are 18 years of age an d above. The Unique Identification Authority of 
India (UIDAI), which is set up under the aegis of Planning Commission, will manage the 
database as well as its updating. 
 (b) Illegal Bangladeshi migrants are not entitl ed to receive ration cards, PAN cards, Voter 
cards etc. Action is taken for cancellation by th e concerned authorities as and when such cases 
are detected. 
 (c) The Central Government is vested with the powers to deport a foreign national under 
section 3(2)(c) of the Foreigners Act, 1946. These powers to identify and deport illegally staying 
foreign nationals have also been delegate d to the State Governments/Union Territory 
Administrations. The detection and deportation of illegally overstaying foreign national and those 
who have entered the country illegally, is a cont inuous process. In the State of Assam, 32 
Foreigners’ Tribunal under  the provisions of Foreigners (Tribunals) Order 1964 have been 
constituted for detection of illegal migrants/f oreigners, and the Central Government is 
reimbursing the expenditure on these to the Government of Assam. A number of measures have 
been taken to check illegal migration and infiltration from Bangladesh which, inter-alia, include:- 

 51
 (i) Construction of border roads,  border fencing and flood lighting; 
 (ii) Round the clock surveillance of the borders by Border Security Force (BSF) patrols 
(both land and reverine); 
 (iii) Setting up of 1185 border outposts, of which 802 have already been established, and 
383 additional outposts have been approved; and  
 (iv) Introduction of modern surveillance equipments gadgets including night vision 
devices. 
 The issue of illegal migration, and deportation on detection has also been taken up with the 
Bangladesh authorities at various levels, and step s have been initiated for coordinated patrolling 
and effective border management, particularly in the unfenced, riverine and other vulnerable 
stretches.

Bangladeshi infiltrators deported to Bangladesh 
 *60. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government is aware about the presence of good number of Bangladeshi 
infiltrators; 
 (b) if so, the efforts being made to check the in filtration identify the settled infiltrators and 
deport them to Bangladesh; and 
 (c) the number of Bangladeshi infiltrators deported to Bang ladesh during the last three 
years? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS  
(SHRI SRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) India’s long and porous border with Bangladesh, 
geographical proximity, family ties and ethn ic similarity, coupled with better economic 
opportunities in India have resulted in illegal migration from Bangladesh. In addition, some 
Bangladeshi nationals, who enter India with valid travel documents, also tend to overstay for 
similar reasons. 
 (b) Central Government is vested with the powers to deport a foreign national under 
section 3(2) (c) of the Foreigners Act, 1946. These Powers to identify and deport illegally 
staying foreign nationals have also been delegated to the state Governments/Union Territory 
Administrations. 
 Initiatives taken to check such illegal immigrat ion and infiltrations from Bangladesh include:- 
 (i) Construction of border roads,  border fencing and flood lighting. 
 (ii) Round the clock surveillance of the borders by Border Security Force (BSF) patrols 
(both land and riverine). 
 (iii) Establishment of 1185 bord er outposts of which 802 outposts have already been set 
up. 
 (iv) Provision of modern surveillance equipm ents including night vision devices to the 
Border Guarding Forces. 
 (v) Bilateral cooperation with the Govern ment of Bangladesh aimed at coordinated 
patrolling and management of borders, especially where fencing is incomplete or not 
feasible. 
 (c) As per the information available, the number of Bangladeshi nationals who came on 
valid travel documents, overstayed and were ther eafter deported during the last three years are 
indicated below:- 
  2005 – 14,916

 (b) and (c) Directorate Genera l of Anti-dumping and Allied Duties (DGAD) initiates anti-

prima-facie evidence of dumping in the country, injury to domestic industry and causal link 
between the dumped goods and injury. Such petitions submitted by domestic industry are

of these cases, preliminary findings have been issued.

Gaping holes in security measures in Mumbai 
 322. SHRI N.K. SINGH: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to  
state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that after 26/11 th ere are still gaping holes in Mumbai armour and 
number of office buildings, Government as well as private, do not have full proof security 
measures; 
 (b) whether it is also a fact that Mumbai se a front remains poorly patrolled and completely 
unguarded; and 
 (c) the steps Government has taken to make Mumbai and other such vulnerable cities full 
proof from terrorists? 

 120
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS  
(SHRI SRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) to (c) ‘Police’ and ‘public order’ being State subjects 
under the Seventh Schedule to the Constitu tion, the State Governments are primarily 
responsible for providing security to the public and public places. However, keeping in view the 
periodic incidents of terrorist violence, particular ly in the metropolitan/urban areas, the Central 
Government has suggested various measures to  the State Governments for preventing such 
incidents and mitigating the impact wherever they occur. These, inter-alia include: strengthening 
of mechanisms for vigilance and gathering of in formation about suspicio us activities at the 
ground level; augmentation of the police forces, including establishment of special 
police/counter terrorism units and re-activation of  the beat constable system; identification of 
vulnerable installations and buildings and strength ening the security arrangements there; setting 
up CCTV based monitoring systems and control rooms; building public awareness and 
mobilizing the involvement and cooperation of public organisations such as market associations, 
etc.; putting in place regulations to  make the provision of basic s ecurity features pertaining to 
access control and surveillance, etc., mandatory in  respect of private es tablishments like malls, 
multiplexes, hotels and other places of public  congregation and high footfalls. The Central 
Government has also circulated a set of indicative guidelines to the State Governments and 
Union Territory Administration in respect of the latter. 
 Apart from the above, the Government is also  implementing a Mega City Policing Scheme in 
various Metropolitan cities, including Mumbai, wherein assistance is being provided for specific 
city policing requirements under the scheme for modern of State Police forces. Security audits of 
vulnerable installations are also being undertaken from time to time. 
 At present, there is a 3 tier arrangement for Coastal Security comprising the State Police for 
the coastal areas and near coastal waters, the Co ast Guard in Territorial Waters and the Navy in 
the High Seas. With a view to strengthening th e arrangements for Coastal Security, the Central 
Government had launched a Supplemental Coastal Security Scheme in 2005, under which 
assistance is being provided to coastal States , including Maharashtra, for setting up Police 
Stations, Outposts, Check Posts and Barracks along with jeeps and motor cycles for patrolling 
along the coast, and provision for 204 patrol boats, which are being procured centrally. The 
States have also been asked to conduct a vulnerability analysis with a view to identifying further 
gaps which may require to be filled up in terms of additional Police Stations, etc. 
 After the incidents in Mumbai, further detailed reviews of the Coastal Security arrangements 
have been carried out, and it has been decided to take a number of additional measures for 
augmenting the assets of the Coast Guard an d the Navy, putting in place institutional 
mechanisms for intelligence sharing and inter-agen cy coordination, registration of boats and 
issue of identity cards to fishermen and the establishing effective Vessel Tracking and Monitoring 
System, etc. 

 121 
 While stressing on the State Governments to ra ise specialized forces/units, it is also been 
decided to establish 4 regional Hubs of the NS G, including one in Mumbai, with a view to 
ensuring immediate and speedy response in the event of any emergency.

Bangladeshis becoming citizens by obtaining ration cards 
 324. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that lakhs of Bangladeshis have illegally immigrated in India and are 
gradually becoming citizens by obtaining Ration Cards etc.; 
 (b) if so, whether Government proposes to check infiltration of such Bangladeshis; and 
 (c) whether any strategy has so far been formul ated by Government to check infiltration of 
Bangladeshis? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS  
(SHRI SRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) to (c) India’s long and porous border with Bangladesh, 
geographical proximity, family ties and ethn ic similarity, coupled with better economic 
opportunities in India have resulted in illegal migration from Bangladesh. In addition, some 
Bangladeshi nationals, who enter India with valid travel documents, also tend to overstay for 
similar reasons. 
 Certain instances of some illegal immigrants fr om Bangladesh having obtained Ration Cards 
through fraudulent means have been reported. As and when such instances are detected, the 
concerned State Governments/Union Territory Administrations take necessary action for 
cancellation of their Ration Cards and further appropriate action as per the provisions of law. 
 Central Government is vested with the powers to deport a foreign national  
under section 3(2) (c) of the Foreigners Ac t, 1946. These powers to identify and  
deport illegally staying foreign nationals have also been delegated to the State 
Governments/Union Territory Administrations. The procedure for the detection and deportation 
of illegal Bangladeshi immigrants has also been set out and circulated to State Governments/UT 
Administrations who are implementing the same on a continuous basis. 
 In order to check illegal immigration and infiltration from Bangladesh, the Government has 
adopted a multi-pronged approach which inter-alia includes the following measures:- 
 (i) Construction of border fenc ing, roads, and floodlighting. 
 (ii) Round the clock surveillance of the borders by Border Security Force. 
 (iii) Setting up of 1185 Border Out Posts (BOPs) along Indo-Bangladesh Border to 
 reduce the inter BOP distan ce for effective border domination, of which 802 BOPs 
have already been established. Sett ing up of remaining 383 BOPs has been 
sanctioned. 
 (iv) Induction of hi-tech surveillance equipment including night vision devices.

States in grip of Naxalites 
 327. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister  of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that nine States in the country endowed with huge natural 
resources have been in the grip of Naxalites where they are even running parallel Governments in 
parts of the State; 
 (b) if so, the details thereof; and 

 136
 (c) whether Government still feels that the situ ation is not so serious as not to warrant the 
raising of a special Central Police Force with air surveillance and air drop capability as also 
access to Central Government Intelligence to assi st concerned State Governments in controlling 
Naxalism in their respective States? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS  
(SHRI SRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) to (c) Naxal violence is reported from parts of the 9 States 
of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, 
Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. However, 4 States of Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and 
Orissa together account for about 86% percent of  the incidents and casualties of civilians and 
security forces. In macro terms, the number of incidents has remained more or less at the same 
level during the last few years. The State-wise break-up of naxal violence and casualities is given 
in the Statement [Refer to the Statement appended to the answer to Unstarred Question 323, 
Part (a) to (c)]. Government remains committed to deal strongly with naxalites indulging in 
crime and violence. The Central Government supplements the efforts of States in several ways. 
This includes deployment of Central paramilitary fo rces to assist the State Police; sanctioning of 
India Reserve battalions; raising of specialized  forces like CoBRA battalions; assistance for 
modernization and upgradation of the State Police and Intelligence agencies through the 
Scheme for Modernization of State Police Fo rces; re-imbursement of security-related 
expenditure under the Security Related Expendit ure Scheme; assistance in training of State 
Police, sharing of Intelligence; facilitating inter-State coordination and assistance in development 
works through a range of schemes of different Ministries. Need based helicopter services are 
also provided to the States for rescue and relief operations. 
Policy for solving insurgency problem in NE 
 328. SHRI BISWAJIT DAIMARY: Will the Minister  of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state:  
 (a) whether there is any policy adopted to solve the insurgency problem in the country 
especially in the North Eastern regions; 
 (b) if so, the details of the policy; 
 (c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
 (d) what are the details of demands of NSCN-IM, NSCN-K, ULFA, NDFB, DHD and 
NLFT; and 
 (e) the details of dialogue between those gr oups which was going on since long back,  
till date any offer has been made by Government for making permanent solution of their 
problem? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI RADHIKA V. 
SELVI): (a) to (c) The Government is suppleme nting the efforts of the State Governments in 
undertaking sustained counter insurgency operations against elements who indulge in violence  

 137
and anti-national activities. At the same time, Go vernment has always been willing to talk to any 
outfit provided it is willing to abjure violen ce and come forward for discussions within the 
framework of the Indian Constitution. 
 The Government has entered into Suspen sion of Operations (SoO)/Cease Fire 
arrangements with National Socialist Council of Nagaland  (Isac/Muivah) [NSCN/IM] and 
National Socialist Council of Nagaland (Khapl ang) [NSCN/K] in Nagaland; United People’s 
Democratic Solidarity (UPDS), Dima Halam Daoga h (DHD) and National Democratic Front of 
Boroland (NDFB) in Assam; Kuki National Or ganization and United People’s Front and its 
constituents in Manipur; and Achik National Volunteer Council (ANVC) in Meghalaya. 
 Dialogue with NSCN(I/M) on their charter of de mands is continuing at the level of Group of 
Ministers (GoM). NSCN(K) has not submitted their charter of demands. NDFB has recently 
agreed to submit its demands within the framewor k of Indian Constitution. Tripartite discussions 
on the demands of DHD are continuing. ULFA has not yet come forward for talks. However, two 
Coys of 28 Bn. of United Liberation Front of Asom (ULFA), who have declared unilateral 
ceasefire, has also not yet submitted their demands. A Memorandum of Settlement (MoS) has 
been signed with National Liberation Front of  Tripura (Nayanbasi) [NLFT(NB)] in December 
2004. However, National Liberation Front of Tripura (Biswamohan) Debbarma) [NLFT/BM] has 
not yet come forward for talks. 
 Tripartite discussions on the demands of the outfits are continuing and it would be 
premature to disclose the details at this stage. 
Foreigners entering India illegally 
 329. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether complaints regarding manipulation s in issuance of visa and passports are on 
the rise in the country; 
 (b) if so, whether several foreigners have entered into India illegally; 
 (c) whether many cases have been detected at the border of Rajasthan and other States; 
and 
 (d) if so, the steps taken by Gove rnment to check such incidents? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS  
(SHRI SRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) to (c) No foreigner is allowed by the immigration 
authorities to enter into the country unless he/she  is in possession of valid travel documents 
including a valid visa. As per available informat ion, 108 cases of forged travel documents were 
detected at Munabao Immigration Check Post (ICP), falling under the district of Barmer in the 
State of Rajasthan, in the year 2008. 

 138
 (d) To ascertain the genuineness of the trav el documents including visas and to detect 
forgeries, the immigration officers at all the ICPs  in the country are prov ided with the specimen 
copies of the travel documents for comparison . They are also provided with Ultra Violet 
Lamps/Magnifying glasses to examine the travel documents including visa s to detect possible 
tampering. In addition, Pass port Reading Machines (PRMs) and Questionable Document 
Examiner (QDX) Machines have also been insta lled at major ICPs. Above all, officers manning 
immigration counters at all the IC Ps are given special training for detection of forged/fake travel 
documents. 
Problems in Tripura due to barbed wire fencing 
 330. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister  of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government has pinpointed the ar eas on the international border of Tripura 
where the barbed wire fencing has been erected about 200 to 500 metre inside Indian territory 
from the zero-point; 
 (b) whether Government is aw are that a good number of fam ilies have been additionally 
affected for this reason and cases of harassment have been occurring almost every where; 
 (c) the details of the incident of firing by BSF personnel on the public, causing deaths and 
injuries on 19.01.09 at Boxonagar in Tripura; and 
 (d) the remedy contemplated for all these cases? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI RADHIKA V. 
SELVI): (a) and (b) Due to topographical configuration, thick habitation, riverine stretches, 
presence of forests and resistance offered by Bangladesh Rifles, the fencing works in some 
patches in Tripura along Indo-Ban gladesh Border has been taken up at a distance of more then 
150 yards from the International border line (zero-point), inside Indian territory. Some location 
specific cases of families affected  by fencing have come to the notice of the Government and 
proper redressal of public grievances are bein g done through remedial measures like financial 
assistance and by providing houses under Indira  Awas Yojana, etc. Proper gates have been 
provided at intervals and timings for opening of ga tes is decided by BSF in consultation with the 
local population, to facilitate the forming activities. 
 (c) and (d) As per the available information, on 19.01.09 the BSF raided a place at 
Dhupuria Bandh (Boxonagar) in Tripura, acting on an information about smuggling of ‘Gamja’. 
During the raid, BSF was attacked by smugglers. In retaliation BSF fired, which has resulted in 
killing of two civilians and injuries to five others including one BSF Jawan. 
 Following remedial measures have been  contemplated for handling such cases:- 
 (i) Troops have been educated not to open fire in populated areas; 

 139
(ii) Troops are advised to associate local police before raiding places for 
contraband/narcotic items and their seizure, particularly in thickly populated areas. 
 (iii) Firing in panic must be avoided. 
 (iv) Troops have been instructed to fire only in self defence. 
NHRC recommendation regarding Nithari killings 
 331. SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether National Human Rights Comm ission has made certain recommendations 
regarding Nithari killings; 
 (b) if so, the details of recommendations; 
 (c) how many recommendations have been accepted by Government; and 
 (d) what is the time-frame given by Go vernment to implement the recommendations? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS  
(DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) and (b) The Nation al Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has 
prepared a Report on Missi ng Children. The Report inter-alia recommends formulation of 
missing persons squads/desks in police stat ions, reiteration of Hon’ble Supreme Court 
guidelines in all police stations, given in Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 610 of 1996 filed by Hori Las  
Vs. Commissioner of Police, Delhi and Others, mandatory reporting, involving Panchayat Raj 
Institutions and NGOs, maintenance of national data base and monitoring by National  
Crimes Record Bureau, revival of State/District Crime Record Bureau, esta blishing of child help 
line, outsourcing preliminary inquiry to NGOs, I- Card for children, poverty alleviation measures, 
role of State Human Rights Commissions, role of me dia, attention to transit points of trafficking 
etc. 
 (c) and (d) Law and Order is a State subject.  It is for the State Governments to take 
appropriate action in every crime. However, the report of the NHRC has be en circulated to all 
State Governments and Union Territories for taking action on the recommendations made by 
NHRC in its Report. However, Ministry of Wo men and Child Development is considering a 
comprehensive legislation to cover the offences against children to create a safe environment for 
children.

 333.  SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether Government has been seized of the suggestion for raising Marine Police wing 
in the coastal States to combat potential infilt rations by terrorists and smugglers through the sea

 (b) if so, the up-to-date status of that suggestion;

 359. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be

allowed to manage provident funds; 
 (b) if so, the details thereo f and the reasons therefor; and

additional contribution towards provident funds? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINIST RY OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI 
OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) to (c) No, Sir. The Provident Fund corpus under Employees’ 
Provident Fund Organisation has been assigned fo r investment to the following four portfolio 
managers on 17.09.2008: 
 (i) HSBC Asset Management Company 
 (ii) ICICI Prudential Asset Management Company 
 (iii) State Bank of India 
 (iv) Reliance Capital Asset Management Company 
 So far, the entire corpus was managed by a single fund manager i.e. State Bank of India. In

 164

on investments is becoming more and more  market driven, Employees’ Provident Fund 
Organisation has decided to get benefited by appointing multi fund managers to bring in 
competition and professionalism in the fund ma nagement process and also help Employees’ 
Provident Fund Organisation in facilitating comparative monitoring. 
 It is expected that this move will bring in be tter yields to Provident Fund corpus and give 
better returns to subscribers in future by instilling competition amongst fund managers.

World Bank findings on Rural Water Supply Schemes 
 369. SHRI VIJAY JAWAHARLAL DARDA: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) the findings of the World Bank Study entitled 
“Review of Effectiveness of Rural Water 
Supply Schemes”, launched in July, 2008; 
 (b) the percentage of functional efficacy of the current rural water schemes, flow of funds 
and expenditure incurred, performance of schemes, cost of supply, household coping strategies 
and costs, etc.; 
 (c) whether any study has been made about the rural household willingness to pay and 
affordability thereof; and 
 (d) if so, the gist of findings? 

 173
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHANDRA 
SEKHAR SAHU): (a) to (d) The study was made by World Bank in ten States covering 38,033 
rural households, which is 0.027 percent of th e total rural households out of the 138,271,559 
households listed as per 2001 census. The number of schemes covered in the sample for the 
study was 765 handpumps and 521 piped water supply schemes. The report has not been 
accepted by Government of India as the sample  studied and analyzed in the report is not 
representative of all the water supply schemes of the country. The major findings related to 
percentage of functional efficacy of the cu rrent rural water schemes, flow of funds and 
expenditure incurred, performance of schemes, cost of supply, household coping strategies and 
costs, rural household willingness to pay and affordability thereof is given in the Statement. 
Statement 
 Major Findings 
 (i) Rural water supply schemes are commonly weak in performance. 
 (ii) Rural households are bearing huge coping. 
 (iii) Supply driven programmes incur large in stitutional costs, substantially raising the 
cost of service provision.  
 (iv) Capital cost of piped water supply schemes is excessive.  
 (v) Operation and maintenance ( O and M) expenditure is inadequate, causing schemes 
to perform below design and shortening their useful life. O and M cost recovery is 
low. 
 (vi) Significant wastage of resources arises from over - provisioning by some schemes, 
defunct schemes and the existence of multiple schemes. 
 (vii) Total cost of piped water schemes is much higher than efficient cost of service 
delivery. 
 (viii) Economies of scale are yet to be realized. 
 (ix) Multi village schemes use more resour ces without commensurate service benefits. 
 (x) There is strong demand and willingn ess to pay and service improvements are 
affordable. 
 The percentage of functional efficacy of the current rural water schemes, flow of funds and 
expenditure incurred, performance of scheme s, cost of supply, household  coping and costs, 
rural household willingness to pay and affordability thereof: 
 (i) Compared to the cost norm s, the capital cost of schemes is found to be higher by 
50% or more in 18% cases. It is higher than the norm by 100% or more in 11% 
cases. 
 (ii) The average annual flow of funds for rural water supply during the period 1997-98 to 
2005-06 for the 10 states ranged from Rs. 0.8 billion (Punjab) to 8.2 billion 
(Maharashtra). 

 174
 (iii) The analysis of survey data on the qu antity of water supplied by schemes shows that 
actual supply is often less than the design, especially in summer.  
 (iv) The total expenditure on rural wate r supply schemes from 1993-94 to 2004-05 (2004-
05 prices) was about Rs. 500 billion. 
 (v) The coping strategies adopted by househol ds  response to the inadequacies of water 
supply include traveling considerable distances and standing in long queues to 
collect water, storing water, incurring expenses on private water sources and 
incurring expenses on repairing public wa ter sources. The average coping cost per 
household is Rs. 81 per month ranging fr om Rs. 32 to Rs. 287 per month across 
different categories of schemes. 
 (vi) A study on willingness to pay provides an indication of the value that consumers 
place on improved water supply and an assessment of the demand for service 
improvement. The underlying  a s s u m p t i o n  i s  t h a t  i f  poor households can pay 3 
percent of their income towards the water bill, then households with higher income 
can also spend 3 percent of their income on the water bill. The average expenditure 
on non-essential items incurred by rural ho use- holds in various states is commonly 
more than the estimated willingness to pay and affordability for a private connection. 
The analysis shows that an additional Rs. 4 billion could be made available each year, 
if households are charged according to their willingness to pay. With these 
resources, the coverage can be increased by 14 percent.

Change of criteria for providing drinking water in Rajasthan 
 †374. SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHAT URVEDI: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
 (a) the details of the categories of villages and hamlets (dhaniva) covered for drinking 
water and the criteria thereof; 
 (b) whether the criteria is appropriate in th e present circumstances in view of extravagant 
of the time and the labour; 
 (c) whether the Government of Rajasthan has be en requesting to change this criteria; and 
 (d) whether Government would consider to changes in the existing criteria? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHANDRA 
SEKHAR SAHU): (a) and (b) The categories of villages and hamlets covered for Accelerated 
Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) are Not Covered (NC)/ No Safe Source (NSS) 
habitation and Partially Covered (PC) habitations. NC/NSS habitations do not have any drinking 
water source/point within 1.6 km of the habitation s in plains or 100 meter elevation in hilly areas, 
or which have a water source but are affected wi th quality problems such as excess salinity, 
iron, fluoride, arsenic or other toxic elements or biologically contaminated. Habitations which 
have a safe drinking water source/point (either private or public) within 1.6 km. in plains and 100 
meter in hill areas but the capacity of the sy stem ranges between 10 lpcd to 40 lpcd, are 
categorised as 
“Partially Covered (PC)”. 
 (c) and (d) Based on consultations with all Stat es, including Rajasthan, the criteria for rural 
water supply has been changed with effect from 01. 04.2009. The National objective is to provide 
every rural person with adequate water for drin king, cooking and other domestic basic needs on 
a sustainable basis. This basic requirement should meet certain minimum water quality 
standards and be available at all times, in all si tuations, in which it is readily and conveniently 
accessible.

 192
 (b) Imported technology does not lead to inte rnational exploitation of labourers. In fact, 
imported technology helps industries in the country to carry on with their businesses and saves 
them time, efforts and resources in developing  the same technologies in-house. Although 
imported technology by itself pr events industry from becoming a global player since it does not 
bring in the latest state-of-the-art technology, In dian industries in some sectors have been able 
to absorb the imported technology successfully an d develop it further indigenously, contributing  
to the technological advancement of the sector. 
 (c) Development of technology has certainly not remained independent of intellectual 
property rights and patents granted in various technical fields. Now, development of any new 
technology usually starts with a patent search in the concerned field to find out about the 
research work already done, so as to avoid reinventing the wheel and formulating the technology 
development problem appropriat ely with a view to add value to existing research and 
development work and generate new intellectual property or patents.

published. According to the Research and Development Statistics published by the Department 
of Science and Technology, patents granted to In dians in India increased from 293 in 1996-97 to 
1907 in 2006-07 and research papers published from India increased from 51002 in 1993 to 68830 
in 2003. Other R and D output indicators are products, processes, import substitutes and design 
prototypes developed and consultancy services rendered by the public and private sector 
institutions and industries as outcome of R and D carried out by them. According to the statistics 
for the year 1999-2000 published by DST, 6056 products, 2233 processes, 2667 import 
substitutes and 4193 design prototypes were developed and 35568 consultancy services were

DR. BARUN MUKHERJI (West Bengal):  Madam Vice-Chairperson, while extending my 
support to the Motion of Thanks on President’s Address, delivered on 12th February, 2009, I 
would like to point out some of my reservations and disappointment on some issues relating to 
the needs of poor and common people. 
The hon. President has rightly raised the most pertinent question ‘Aam Aadmi ko kya mila?’ 
But, Aam Aadmi is hardly convinced of the benefits that have been accrued to him as suggested 
in her Address. The Government may feel happy and proud to publicise that, ‘It has acted on 
nearly all the commitments made to the pe ople through the National Common Minimum 
Programme.’ But, quite a few vital commitments lik e ‘right to education’ or ‘reservation for 
women in Lok Sabha and State Legislatures’ are still confined in Bills as th ey have been merely 
introduced in Parliament. The Bills, as such, may sound vibrating for election campaign. But the 
people’s aspirations are not fulfilled merely by introduction of Bills. Madam, more than 30 per 
cent of our population is still illiterate and the women are deprived of much needed social and 
economic rights. Even the question may be raised as to how far the right to work, as has been 
guaranteed through the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, is implemented. 

 246 
 Unemployment and poverty levels are stead ily rising. Due to recent global economic 
meltdown we have already lost about 5 lakh jo b s .  I n  s p i t e  o f  a n  A c t ,  m i l l i o n s  o f  w o r k e r s  
belonging to the unorganised sector are still depriv ed of minimum social security provisions and 
also a large number of people are miserably de pendent on a meagre income of Rs. 20 a day. 
Unfortunately, all these hard realities are not reflected in President’s Address. It has, rather, tried 
to list out a handful of works done by the UPA Government during its near completed tenure. 
The Address, Madam, has thus become more lik e an election manifesto than the realistic 
assessment of the situation concerning the Aam Aadmi.  
Madam, in spite of the claims of increase in  agricultural production, the country is now 
depending more and more on imported foodgrains which will not speak well of our food security. 
Moreover, if the production is so high, why could not more quantity of foodgrains be distributed 
through the PDS? 
The newly initiated National Rural Health Missio n is far from eradicating diseases of millions 
of our people. On the contrary, health care facilities of international standards are available in our 
country, but at such a high cost that it is far beyond the reach of the common man. This basic 
inequality in our society in respect of money, heal th, education and other social benefits is still a 
positive hindrance to inclusive growth that the Government claims to have achieved. The Special 
Economic Zones, which the UPA Government claims to be a unique achievement, is, in fact, the 
biggest land-grab move in the recent times. It is discriminating in nature. It is creating a special 
privileged group that enjoys many undue exemptions from taxes and fees. In the name of export 
promotion and employment generation, the SEZ people are exploiting the resources of the 
country and are enjoying undue privileges. The sooner it is abolished the better would be the 
prospects of inclusive growth. Although the Indo -US nuclear deal has be en highly praised as, 
“One of the manifestations of the transformation in our relationship with the United States of 
America”. We are afraid, it would eventually prove as a detrimental to the interest of our country. 
The US nuclear reactor business is heading to flourish at our cost. At the same time, the 
strategic partnership with the US would eventua lly tarnish India’s traditional image of a non-
aligned country and would adversely affect  our independent foreign policy. The UPA 
Government’s high hopes that ‘our young people have never been more confident about the 
future’ as manifested in the Address is rather very difficult to accept. Unemployment, poverty, 
price rise, ill health, illiteracy, deficiency in the PDS, continuing threats of job loss are constantly 
haunting our young generation. It is better to be  more realistic in our assessment and find out 
means of socialistic reconstruction of our country. Thank you very much.
