 †507. DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
  SHRI SHIVANAND TIWARI: 
 Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 (a) whether it is a fact that Food and Agricu lture Organization has published a report that 
around one billion people are starving in the world; 
 (b) if so, whether it is also a fact that 65 pe r cent of this population is in seven countries 
and India is one of them; 
 (c) if so, whether Government has found out the population of starving persons in India; 
and 
 (d) if so, the population thereof?  
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY): 
(a) No Sir. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.
  

 210
 The report titled ‘The State of Food Insecurity in the World 2008’ published by FAO states, 
“Worldwide, 848 million people suffered from chronic hunger in 2003-05 ”. It discusses about 
chronic hunger not starvation. There is concep tual difference between chronic hunger and 
starvation. Chronic hunger is long term problem re lated to inadequate food availability leading to 
problem of undernourishment; whereas, starvation is acute hunger problem in short-run, where 
food is not available. These are basically acute v/s chronic problems. 
 (b) Yes Sir.  
 The report further states that of undernourished people, 65 percent live in only seven 
countries and India is one of them. 
 (c) and (d) The methodology and terminology used in the FAO report and in India is 
different. Chronic hunger data as defined in FAO report is not available. Whereas, the Chapter 4 
on Nutrition and Social Safety Net of Eleventh Five Year Plan (Volume II) Document states the 
problem in terms of protein-energy malnutrition  (PEM). According to National Family Health 
Survey-2 (NFHS-2), as much as 36 percent of the adult population of India had a Body mass 
index (BMI) below 18.5 (the cut off for adult malnutrition) in 1998-99. This share had fallen to 33 
percent of the population in 2005-06.

 519.  SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: 
  SHRI DARA SINGH: 
 Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD TRAN SPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether in India maximum penalty for road contractors is forfeiture of his deposit 
amount and black listing of his company instead of sending him to jail as in USA; 
 (b)  if so, whether Government is aware of po or construction of roads all along National or 
State Highways particularly in Delhi’s potholed roads including Janakpuri Flyover which was to

 (d)  the remedial steps taken by Central Road  Research Institute to ensure high durability

 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI K.H. MUNIAPPA): (a) Yes, Sir. The maximum penalty for non-performing of

 529.  SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether India accounts for 10 per cent of  the total road accidents in the world and 
International Road Federation has set a target of reducing fatal road accidents in India by 50 per 
cent by 2010; 
 (b)  if so, the details thereof; 
 (c)  the effective measures taken by Governme nt to check the increasing number of road 
accidents; 
 (d)  whether Government has any proposal  to introduce Highway Traffic Management 
System throughout the country; and 
 (e)  if so, the details thereof? 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINIST RY OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI K.H. MUNIAPPA): (a) and (b) No Sir. As per the data published in World 
Road Statistics 2008, by the International Road Federation, for the year 2005, the total Road 
accidents in the World were 78,84,804, of which, India’s share was only 5.6 Percent. 
 (c) The Safety of road users is primarily  the responsibility of the concerned State 
Government. This Department has, however, taken several steps to improve road safety for the 
road users which are as under: 
 (i) Road safety is the integral part of ro ad design at the planning stage for National 
Highways/Expressways. 

 240 
 (ii) Various steps to enhance road safety such as road furniture, road markings/road 
signs, introduction of Highway Traffic Ma nagement System using Intelligent Transport 
System, enhancement of discipline among contractors during construction, road 
safety audit on selected stretches, have  been undertaken by National Highways 
Authority of India (NHAI). 
 (iii) Refresher training to Heavy Motor Vehicle drivers in the unorganized sector. 
 (iv) Involvement of NGOs for road safety ac tivities by Department of Road Transport and 
Highways and NHAI. 
 (v) Setting up of Model Driving Training School in the country by Department of Road 
Transport and Highways. 
 (vi) Publicity campaign on road safety aw areness through audio-vi sual-print media by 
Department of Road Transport and Highways. 
 (vii) Institution of National Award for voluntary organizations/individual for outstanding 
work in the field of road safety by Department of Road Transport and Highways. 
 (viii) Tightening of safety standards of vehicles. 
 (ix) Provision of cranes and ambulances to various State Governments/NGOs under 
National Highway Accident Relief Service Scheme. National Highways Authority of 
India also provides ambulances at a dist ance of 50 Km. on each of its completed 
highways under its Operation and Maintenance contracts. 
 (x) Widening and improvements  of National Highways from 2 lanes to 4 lanes and 4 lanes 
to 6 lanes etc. 
 (d) and (e) National Highways of Authority of  India, as a part of the Road Safety Zone 
concept under Asian Development Bank (ADB) fu nded Projects, is planning to implement 
Highway Traffic Management System (HTMS) on  a section of approx. 150 km on East West 
Corridor in the states of Madhya Pradesh and U ttar Pradesh. Apart from this, provisions of 
HTMS are being included in all the Build, Oper ate and Transfer (BOT) projects, being awarded 
under new Model Concession Agreement (MCA). The details are given in the Statement.

Cruise shipping policy 
 531.  SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
  SHRIMATI RENUBALA PRADHAN: 
 Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD TRAN SPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
 (a)  whether Government has formulated cruise shipping policy to promote tourism; 
 (b)  if so, the details thereof; 
 (c)  whether it is proposed to develop ex clusive docking facilities for cruise liners at 
important ports in the country by the Central Government; and 
 (d)  if so, the details thereof, inter-alia indicating such facilities that are proposed to be 
developed in the ports in Orissa coast to promote this tourism in the State? 
 THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS  
(SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Go vernment of India approved Cruise Shipping 
Policy on 22/9/2008. Cruise Shipping would be a path breaking development in India’s effort of 
carve a prominent space in world tourism and it would showcase India as a major source and 
destination of world tourism. With the implemen tation of this policy, the growth in diverse 
sectors will improve and it will earn precious fore ign exchange for the country. It will not only 
generate enormous employment opportunities but will also promote people to people contact, 
which will enhance India’s friendly ties with foreign countries. 
 Various features of cruise shipping policy include conducive fiscal regime, development of 
facilities at Ports and connectivity through rail, road transport, air and metro, quick completion of 
immigration formalities, hassle free custom clearance and proper waste disposal system 
ensuring Cleaner Ocean. 
 (c) and (d) Cochin Port, New Mangalore Port , Mumbai Port, Chennai Port and Tuticorin 
Port have initiated proposals for developing dedicated passenger cum cruise terminals for cruise 
vessels. In so far as Orissa concerned, there is only one Major Port namely Paradip Port. 
Presently, there is no proposal to develop exclusive docking facilities for cruise liners in this port. 
With regard to non-major Ports, as per Indian Ports Act, 1908, these ports are under the 
jurisdiction of respective Maritime States.

Demand to restore pensionary benefits to RBI Employees 
 SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala):  Sir, I rise to draw the attention of the House and also 
of the Government to the countrywide strike by almost the entire workforce, 25,000 employees 
and officers, of the country’s central bank, the Re serve Bank of India, which is going to take 
place tomorrow on 20th February 2009. 
 The strike has been forced upon them by  the Government by imposing unilateral and 
arrogant decision to curtail the pension bene fits of the RBI employees decided by the RBI 
Management Board and implemented since 2003. In 2003, the RBI Board decided to update the 
pension payment of the retired employees following the pay revision of the regular employees. In 
2008, the Government forced the RBI management to withdraw such updated pension benefits 
for the employees and officers revised in 2003 following the regular pay revision of the 
employees. This resulted in reduction of pension by Rs. 1,000 to Rs. 6,000 for around 4,000 
retired employees; and such forcible withdrawal of the revision of pension benefits is going to 
adversely affect the pension rights of the existing employees as well. 
 It is ridiculous that while the Central Pay Commission allowed upward revision of pension 
benefits for the retirees in Government serv ices, how could the Government deny similar 
provision for pension-revision for the RBI employees, even when RBI management has managed 
the same from its own resources without any budgetary support? I demand that the Government 
must review its unjust and irrational decision in this regard forthwith in consultation with the 
employees and officers’ association of RBI to avoid aggravation of industrial unrest in RBI.

The Central Industries Security Force (Amendment) Bill, 2008 
 THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): Sir, I beg to move: 
That the Bill further to amend the Central Indust rial Security Force Act, 1968, be taken into 
consideration. 
 Sir, this is a Bill to amend the Central Indust rial Security Force Act to enable the CISF to 
extend security cover to establishments in the private sector, as well as, in the joint sector. 

 314
There are a number of establishmen ts in the joint sector, as well as, in the private sector which 
are important both to the economy and to the s ecurity of the country. Some examples are oil 
installations, refineries, coal mi nes, ports, etc., and, therefore, we think that the times demand 
that the CISF be, probably, extended to these establishments also. That is the main purpose of 
this amendment. The CISF is one of our best-trained and best-equipped forces today. It has a 
strength of 1,12,534 officers and men. It is de ployed in 280 establishments. We have permitted 
further raising of the CISF to 1,45,000. We think, with the demands that are coming in, the 
strength of this Force can be raised over a period of time and deployed. The CISF, of course, will 
continue to provide security to the public sector  establishments and many more will be covered. 
There will be no, I will repeat there will be no, question of reducing the CISF cover to the public 
sector. The first claim to the CISF will be of the Government and the public sector. As the Force 
is raised and its strength increases, we will re spond to requests from the joint sector and the 
private sector; and depending upon the importan ce of that establishment we will consider 
extending the CISF security cover. It will not happen overnight because the Force has to be 
raised. We will also do a risk analysis before we  decide to accept the engagement. We will rely 
on modern technology and modern gadgetry. We will, of course, give preference to areas which 
are, today, more vulnerable like naxaliteaffected areas or areas more vulnerable to terrorist 
attacks. We are grateful to the Standing Comm ittee which has broadly endorsed the Bill. The 
Standing Committee has, of course, taken note of  the statements made by the Home Secretary 
and the officials of the Ministry  of Home Affairs and said that the CISF must remain only a 
security force and must not intervene in land di sputes or industrial disputes. That goes without 
saying. The CISF has never intervened in land di sputes or industrial disputes or law and order 
disputes. Its business is to ensure the security of  the establishment. If any dispute arises, that 
will be taken up by the local police which is responsible for law and order, and the CISF will 
remain completely neutral and stay away from all these disputes. There are standard procedures 
which are in place for many years. This is led by an officer of a very high rank, the DG rank. We 
are strengthening the supervisory ranks also. I would request the hon. Members to kindly 
discuss and pass this Bill.

 SHRI S. S. AHLUWALIA: Sir, before we adjourned for lunch I was speaking on CISF Bill.

tier system in security, wherever you are prov iding security, you train their watch and ward

attack or which will be dealing with the terrorist attacks only and they should be deputed on the 
strategic points. Otherwise, what will happen is, once you give the duty of CISF to the watch 
and ward there will be lot of hassles or a lot of problems. Let the other problems be dealt with by 
the private companies themselves and their people  should be trained by CISF and for that you 
must charge them, you must take money from th em and you give a well trained combating unit 
so that they can protect the establishment from  any terrorist attack. Sir, for that, women and 
men, both should be trained because in a compan y like Infosys you will find that there are plenty 
of women IT engineers who are working and when  you are facing this, the terrorist may, the 
Fidayeen may come in the shape of a lady suicide bomber or suicide attack team. To deal with 
them women also are needed. I believe that ther e are enough women in the CISF so that they 
can get training. Sir, for training and for their skilled development you must have sophisticated 
weapons also. I do not know, today we are having  maximum SLRs or automatic rifles or we are 
having in some places AK-47 or so. The terrorists  are using the latest technology and the latest 
weapons. To combat with them we should have that weapon also. When we are deputing these 
people to combat terrorists, they must be provid ed with that type of weapons so that they can 
combat efficiently. Sir, modern communication is required. We have seen that we do not have 
the modern communication facilities. We have lear nt from 26/11. They were using Blackberries. 
They were using satellite phones. They were using a plenty of other things. Recently, a new virus 
has attacked the software and has paralysed the whole communication system in Tajikistan. We 
should learn from all these thin gs and virus-proof, foolproof firewall software should be made 
available for communications system in the CISF.

India has an observer status. India is looking forward to becoming a full member of the FATF. 
However, it is something which has gone largely unreported in the Indian media that Pakistan is 
not a member of the FATF. On 20th February 2008, the FATF had occasion to point out that it

unscrupulous means, unscrupulous roots, and, money-laundering is one of the important

investigate, we have, rather see to it that they act expeditiously and see that the objective of the 
Act is not frustrated otherwise. 
 The second point he raised was about the tr aining of staff of banks to deal with the 
situation. Here, I would just like to add only in one sentence that the banks carry out regular 

 356 
programmes for providing necessary training to st aff at different levels. That is the reason why 
we have been successfully come down to core  banking solutions in many banks. The core 
banking solution is increasing in all branches of  banks. The concerned officials of the banks are 
well trained. If I were to say so, if one fake In dian currency note pass es through their hands, 
without even using machines, they are able to detect that. 
 Sir, I am, at the same time, conscious of the fact which hon. Member Shri Tiwariji made 
that there has been a case. But, Sir, that is where you can come across  a situation like that 
anywhere. You can come across with dishonest persons anywhere and you really cannot make 
laws to that extent to deal with every act of di shonesty. Though, we have a plethora of laws to 
deal with such situations, the case that he cited was where a bank employee was involved in this 
and it was detected. He would appreciate that it was detected by the bank staff only. The banks 
are mandated to file fortnightly reports about an y incident which come to their notice. If any 
receipt of fake Indian currency note is received, they have to report to the Reserve Bank of India. 
The Reserve Bank of India has very stringent laws  to deal with situation where a bank does not 
even file a return. The officers in the bank and dealing hands deal with it thoroughly. Sir, again, it 
is an on-going process. They have their traini ng agencies. They have their training colleges. 
They have their training institutes where, on a regular basis, the necessary training is imparted to 
the people to ensure that their training does not or their skill is not rendered obsolete at any 
stage. 
 Sir, the third point he made was about the abuse of the Participatory Notes. In this 
connection, I would like to say, the ambit of the reporting regime is widened. We have included 
very many other agencies not only just banking and non-banking financial companies but also 
other intermediaries. The definition has been widened to include very many, including the Stock 
Exchanges. But, coming to the Participatory No tes, my hon. friend would appreciate that 
Participatory Notes — he knows more than me — are those instruments which are issued by the 
FIIs to investors abroad. Sir, the FIIs collect mo ney and invest that in India. The Participatory 
Notes are regulated by the jurisdictions abroad where they are issued and there are stringent 
laws. We have elaborate law in force. Sir, only  those Participatory Notes are recognised here 
which are issued by the regulated jurisdiction there, not otherwise. A reference has been made 
as to what the SEBI has done about it. Since 2003, the SEBI has provided that the Participatory 
Notes can be issued in only well regulated jurisdictions. I repeat this point only for the sake of 
adding emphasis to it. In this case also, a mont hly return has been prescribed by the SEBI for 
FIIs to file it regarding information containing the details about the holder of the Participatory 
Notes and the amount invested. Sir, the SEBI, I say with a sense of satisfaction, has not come 
across even a single case where it has been said that the Participatory Notes have been abused 
or misused.  

 357 
 The participatory notes are not issued or traded in India. As I said earlier, they are issued 
abroad. The SEBI cannot control the issuance of such participatory notes abroad. It can only 
regulate them. And, they are, indeed, regulate d. India can be proud of the fact that we  
have strong, independent and autonomous regulato ry bodies, whether it is the Central Bank, in 
the form of the Reserve Bank of India, or, it is the IRDA, or, it is the SEBI. Therefore, I will urge 
that we need not really entertain any doubt abou t the abuse of the participatory notes in this 
process.  
 The other point that the hon. Member rais ed was regarding the German Bank. The hon. 
Member asked why is it so that India has not ap proached them. I would only like to inform that 
the Central Board of Direct Taxes is pursuing the matter with them and so is our Ambassador to 
Germany. They are pursuing that matter ther e. The hon. Member also asked about the 
regulatory mechanism in the Act. Perhaps, by ‘regulatory’ he meant as to how the Act is 
working. I would like to inform in this connection and it would be suffice to say that all the 
authorities under the Act, whether they are adju dicating authorities, or, they are appellate 
tribunals, or, the Directors, or, any one, different roles are assigned to different authorities under 
a well-defined, elaborately worked out piece of legislation, taking care that while we are 
stringent in taking action against any violation of the law as far it involves tainted money; at the 
same time, taking care that the well-accepted norm s of criminal jurispru dence are not violated 
anywhere, that law has been framed, all the auth orities are in place. Sir, maybe, not very 
necessary to give this information, but when I say that all the authorities are in place, the number 
of cases under investigation, at present, is 58. The provisional attachment is in 28 cases. The 
value of property against this is Rs. 53,44,34,936/-. 
 Hon. Member, Shrimati Jayanthi Natarajan, made two points. And, those are the two 
points, where I said that we presently find ours elves unable to agree to those recommendations 
of the Standing Committee. The first one relates to exempting proceeds of  market manipulation 
from confiscation. In this case, the Government has considered this point at length. And, our 
opinion, which I would like to share with the hon.  House, is that the proceeds of crime to the 
bona fide owner of the property may also arise in re spect of several other predicate offences, 
other than the stock manipulation and inside training, such as, robbery, dacoity and forgery, 
etc. Hence, if we were to change the definition , if we were to incorporate the suggestion of the 
Standing Committee, then, it coul d lead to a situation that may not be desirable to have this 
provision because many, many more  claims could come up. Sir, wh at we feel is that such a 
provision would not be in line with the basic st ructure of the Prevention of Money Laundering 
Act. However, the confiscated proceeds of crim e can be disposed of by the Government. That 
is provided in the Act. It can be disposed of by  the Government at any time in such a manner as 
it deems appropriate. And, theref ore, because of this provision, the Government can refund the 
confiscated property on the advice of the SEBI in  cases where the predicate offences relate to 
stock manipulations and inside trading. And, ther efore, without having a provision like that  — 

 358 
because that would open the floodgates of many other claims and would even lead to some sort 
of frustration of some objectives of the Ac t — the Government can be approached and the 
Government can always release that property when the occasion like this arises. 
 As I said earlier, we have to strike a balanc e between the two. Therefore, if the need is so 
felt, the Government can always do it. 
 The second point which she referred to was th e need to have a threshold in case of fake 
Indian currency notes. I for one,  Sir, have come across these kinds of cases. Unfortunately, the 
law is like that. Sir, the problem really lies not wi th this provision, but it is elsewhere. And an 
amendment to the IPC is needed. Under the law, as I understand it — Mr. Ravi Shankar Prasadji 
will bear me out for this — is that even possession  of one fake currency note is an offence. If, 
per chance, I go to the market and somebody hand s out one fake currency note to me, as the 
law stands today, even that is an offence. But, if you put some sort of threshold, then, the basic 
thing about which many hon. Members of this House have referred to will be taken care of. I can 
assure the House the number of fake Indian curr ency notes, which have been seized from time 
to time, is not alarming at all. There is no ca use for concern about that. But, nevertheless, the 
fact remains that there are forces inimical to us which would like to pump in such money. In what 
way they do it? They split it into different part s and do it. They may flood the market. Therefore, 
the need to have a threshold would not be really called for, particularly, because in criminal 
jurisprudence, for every offence, the mens rea, the guilty mind is necessary. That is important. 
Therefore, one need not really have any thre shold provision. She would agree with me, I 
suppose she is agreeing with me that it is fo r these reasons that this provision has not been 
incorporated there. 
 There was a general discussion about the role  that dirty money plays in our social and 
political life. Those are the issues for which I do n’t consider myself competent to be discussing. 
At the moment, we are discussing the provisions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Bill. I 
suppose, it is the clarion call given by Shri Ravi  Shankar Prasadji that all the parties should get 
together to deal with the menace, which has become a scourge of the society today. We have to 
get together to fight that out. All I would like to say is that the passing of this law today would 
really widen the scope... (Interruptions).. With the passing of this law, we can proudly go to  
Asia-Pacific Group as also the Financial Action Task Force, the International Organisation which 
is coordinating the efforts in the field of anti-mon ey laundering. Sir, with the observer status that 
we have at present today, I am sure, we will soon become a regular member, thereof, and we 
will be second to none in dealing with this problem and through that many other problems which 
were referred to would be solved. 
 With these words, I thank the hon. Members fo r extending an all out support to this Bill. 
Thank you.

National Mission on Medicinal Plants 
*82. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA:†† 
 SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has recently approved a Centrally sponsored 
National Mission on Medicinal Plants; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether most of the medicinal plants are on the verge of 
extinction and herbal industry has been affected adversely; and 
(d) if so, the facts thereof and the steps taken by Government to 
encourage farmers to grow more medicinal plants to protect the herbal 
industry? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) 
to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The Government has recently approved a new Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme of National Mission on Medicinal Plants with a total 
outlay of Rs. 630 crores for implementation during the 11th Plan by 
National Medicinal Plants Board. The scheme aims at supporting market 
driven cultivation of medicinal plants prioritized on the basis of their 
demand in the AYUSH and Herbal industry and will be implemented in a 
mission mode in selected clusters through growers' cooperatives, self 
help groups, producer companies, etc. with backward and forward linkages 
for nurseries, post-harvest management, marketing and certification. The 
activities for which financial assistance is available under the scheme 
are the following: 
• Nurseries in public and private sector for quality planting material 
• Cultivation of species that are in demand in AYUSH and Herbal industry 
• Support Post Harvest Management infrastructure like warehouses, 
processing units, setting up/ upgradation of herbal mandies 

2 
• Market Intelligence 
• Marketing Support 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Prof. Alka Balram 
Kshatriya. 

3 
• Organic Certification 
• Quality Testing 
• Crop Insurance 
• Management Support 
Under the Scheme, the State Governments are required to formulate 
Action Plans with approval of State Level Steering Committee before these 
are considered for approval by the Central Government. During the 11th 
Five Year Plan, it is proposed to provide financial assistance for 
coverage of 80,000 – 1,00,000 hect. of area under medicinal plants in the 
clusters to be identified by the State Governments. The scheme also aims 
at increasing the share of value added items in the export of medicinal 
plants and products besides creating 6 crore mandays of employment. 
The medicinal plants, like other group of plants and animals, are 
threatened largely due to degradation of forests owing to various 
anthropogenic factors. There have been reports received from some 
industries also regarding non- availability of some medicinal plants in 
required quantities. There is, however, no information about the 
medicinal plants being on verge of extinction. 
The National Medicinal Plant Board is also implementing a Central 
Sector Scheme for Rs. 320/-  crores under the 11th Five Year Plan under 
which support is provided to the S tate governments for conservation and 
plantation of medicinal plants in forest areas so as to augment 
availability of medicinal plants which are of conservation concerns and 
are otherwise in high demand by the herbal industry. The Board has so far 
sanctioned projects for conservation and plantations covering about 39983 
hectare land in forest area and other public lands. In addition, projects 
have been sanctioned to about 6800 farmers covering approximately 40,000 
hectare land for cultivation of identified medicinal plants and thereby 
augment their availability for the herbal industry.

Substandard drugs 
*87. SHRI A. ELAVARASAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many drugs produced by the well known 
pharma companies are substandard; 
(b) if so, whether Government has conducted any survey to find out the 
quality of medicines produced by well known, leading pharma companies; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the action taken by Government against those companies whose 
products were found substandard? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) 
to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) There are no reports that many drugs produced by the well known 
pharma companies have been reported to be substandard. The drug 
manufacturers are required to test each batch of the finished product in 
their own laboratory or laboratories approved by the State Licensing 
Authority before release of drugs for sale. The drug products are 
manufactured under licenses granted by the State Licensing Authorities 
after ensuring that they comply with the conditions of the license. 
Manufacturing premises are inspected by State Drugs Inspectors to ensure 
that they conform to Good Manufacturing Practices. However, because of 
long distance transportation, wide variation of temperature and improper 
storage, deterioration may occur in certain cases. The check on the 
quality of the drugs marketed in the country is earned out through random 
sampling by the Drugs Inspectors appointed by various State Governments. 
(b) and (c) No survey has been conducted to find out the quality of 
drugs produced by any specified category of manufacturers by the 
Government of India. However, it has been decided to conduct a study to 
know the extent of spurious drugs in the country, for which samples have 
already been collected from across the country. 
(d) The State Licensing Authorities take action against the 
manufacturers whose products are found not of standard quality depending 
upon the nature of defects under the provision of the Drugs and Cosmetics 
Act and Rules made thereunder.

Government. The State Governments are responsible for enforcing quality

I now come to the question raised by the hon. Member. The hon. Member

DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS: Sir, if the hon. Member has any information 
about any specific product or any company and he shares that with us, we 
will, definitely, inspect it. Nevertheless, I would like to say that in 
the last couple of years we have taken a number of steps to streamline 
the process for checking spurious drugs or adulterated drugs or 
sub-standard drugs or the drugs which are not of standard quality. Sir, 
these are the four categories in India. I would like to say that we, in 
fact, amended the Drugs and Cosmetics Act last year, in the last Session, 
whereby we recommended stricter penalties, legal and penal implications 
if anybody is found selling spurious drugs or adulterated drugs. I would 
like to say, Sir, that the amendment was passed by both the Houses. It is 
now there to be notified. The penalty for anybody selling a spurious drug 
by which some person dies or grievously injured is minimum 10 years 
imprisonment and maximum life imprisonment. So, it is there in the Act. 
Plus the individual or the company has to pay a fine of Rs.10 lakh or

*81. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 

39 
(a) whether Government plans to check sugar exports via advance 
licence; 
(b) if so, whether under this licence scheme sugar millers will have 
to obtain his Ministry's release orders for shipping out any consignment; 
(c) whether India is still facing shortage of sugar; 
(d) whether Government is also planning to extend Release Orders (RO) 
dispensation to cover re -export commitments under Advance Licence (AL) 
scheme and the scheme also requires mills to re-export one tonne of white 
sugar for every 1.05 tonnes of raw-sugar they import duty free; and 
(e) if so, to what extent it has helped to check sugar exports? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI 
SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (e) The Central Government in its decision dated 
28.01.2009 has allowed sugar mills to import raw sugar under Advance 
Authorization Scheme upto 30.09.2009 and permitted sugar factories to 
sell processed raw sugar in the domestic market and fulfill export 
obligation on 'ton-to-ton' basis. A wastage of 5% has been allowed under 
Standard Input Output Norms (SION- 52) on import of raw sugar and export 
of white sugar. 
The sugar production in India is cyclic in nature; two- to-three years 
of high production are followed by two- to-three years of low production. 
The production of sugar is likely to be less than the consumption but 
keeping in view large opening stock in the beginning of the season, there 
would be adequate availability of sugar in the current sugar season. 
The requirement of obtaining release orders for export of sugar under 
Open General Category has been re- introduced with effect from 01.01.2009 
and for export of sugar under Advance Authorization Scheme with effect 
from 13.02.2009. This would enable the Government to judiciously issue 
export release orders whether under Open General License or under Advance 
Authorization Scheme. 
Since the requirement of obtaining export release order has been re-
introduced a few days back, it is too early to assess its impact.

Violation of PNDT Act 
*88. SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of female foetuses aborted in the country in violation 
of Pre- Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PNDT) Act in the last two years, 
State-wise; and 
(b) the details of action taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) 
and (b) Sex determination techniques have been in use in India since 1975 
primarily for the determination of genetic abnormalities. However, these 
techniques were widely misused to determine the sex of the foetus and 
subsequent abortions if the foetus was found to be female. 
Studies indicate that sex determination tests are conducted and female 
foeticide carried out surreptitiously with the active connivance of the 
service providers and t he persons seeking such services. Unlike other 
cases, both parties gain through such complicity, i.e. while the service 
seekers are able to get rid of the unwanted female foetus, the service 
providers benefit financially. The absence of witness to such unholy 
alliance or evidence thereto makes detection and compilation of data 
regarding such violations of the Act difficult. However, according to the 
National Crime Record Bureau (NCRB), 125 and 96 cases were registered 
during 2006 and 2007 respectively for foeticide. 
With a view to overcoming such circumvention of the law, the 
implementing agencies, as also the NGOs and other organisations, are 
encouraged to employ decoy customers for trapping such unscrupulous 
service providers and book cases against them under the law. 
Further, the Government has taken action on strengthening the Pre -
Conception & Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act (PC & PNDT Act) as well 

42 
as creating awareness on the issue through various IEC mechanisms. Some 
of the steps taken by the Government to improve the Child Sex Ratio in 
the Country are: 
• Constitution of the Central Supervisory Board under the Chairmanship 
of Union Minister of Health & Family Welfare, whose function, inter 
alia, is to advise the Central Government on policy matters relating 
to use of pre- natal diagnostic techniques, sex selection techniques 
and against their misuse and to create public awareness against the 
practice of pre- conception sex selection and pre- natal determination 
of sex of foetus leading to female foeticide; 

43 
• Constitution of the National Inspection & Monitoring Committee (NIMC) 
for undertaking field visits periodically across the country. 
• Constitution of the National Support & Monitoring Cell (NSMC) for 
effective implementation of the Act. 
• The reports of NIMC and NSMC are forwarded to the concerned State/UT  
Governments with the request to take appropriate remedial action for 
plugging  
any shortcomings, including initiation of penal proceedings against 
the violators pointed out in the reports, since implementation of the 
Act rests with the State/UT Governments. 
• Provisions have also been made for sensitising the Judiciary and the 
public prosecutors. 
• Publication of Annual Reports, Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs), 
• On-Line Complaint registration facility on the Ministry's Website. 
• Dedicated website for PC & PNDT Activities, i.e. 'pndt.gov.in', for 
online filing  
of  'Form F' by clinics and such retrieval of such data at District, 
State and National level. 
• Organising sensitisation workshops/ seminars, launching of 'Save the 
Girl Child' campaign, seeking cooperation from the NGOs/religious 
leaders, etc.. 
• Further, under the National Rural Health Mission, Auxiliary Nursing 
Midwife (ANM) and Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) are being 
sensitised on the issue. Also, funds have been provided to all 
States/UTs under the Rural Child Health programme for implementation 
of the Act and related activities. 
• The Government is open to further strengthen the PC & PNDT Act, 1994 
and the Rules framed thereunder to make them more stringent.

Use of toxic chemicals in food and vegetables 
†*90. SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHATURVEDI: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether toxic chemicals are being used in fresh foodstuff and 
sweets; 
(b) whether Formaldehyde, Boric and Benzoic acids, industrial colour 
sulphur dioxide etc. are being used fearlessly in order to keep 
vegetables fresh in look and colour; 
(c) whether use of these chemicals is increasing liver, kidney and 
cancer-related diseases along with mental retardation and hinders the 
physical and mental growth of children; 
(d) whether gas is used for making wine, and also for ripening and 
drying of fruits, which is increasing respiratory and heart related 
diseases; and 
(e) if so, the measures being, taken to stop this practice at 
processing and marketing levels? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) 
and (b) No, Sir. The salts of benzoie acid and sulphur dioxide are 
permitted to be used for selected food for specific purposes under PFA 
Rules, 1955. The permitted levels have been fixed after due consideration 
of safety. The use of industrial colours in vegetables is not permitted. 
(c) Maximum limits for use of various chemicals have been prescribed 
in the PFA Act and Rules. Within the prescribed limit, such use is 
considered to be safe for human beings. 
(d) The PFA Rules, 1955, prohibits use of carbide gas for ripening of 
fruits. The State Governments have been requested to keep vigil on 
quality of fruits for ensuring that they are not ripened artificially by 
use of carbide gas. The use of sulphur dioxide is permitted in alcoholic 
wines, dehydrated fruits and dehydrated vegetables upto a prescribed 
level and permitted levels have been fixed after due consideration of  
safety. According to ICMR, sulphites beyond permissible level are known 
to trigger asthma in sensitive individuals, while there is no information 
on causing heart related problems. 
(e) The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and Rules, 1955 
have been enacted to prevent adulteration in food stuffs. Food articles 
sold in the market are required to conform to the specifications laid 
down under PFA Rules, 1955. The implementation of Act and Rules is 

46 
entrusted with the Food (Health) Authorities of the States/U.Ts. Random 
samples of various food articles are taken by enforcement staff of the 
State Governments and penal action is taken against the offenders where 
the samples do not conform to the prescribed standards. 
The State Governments have been requested from time to time to check 
the malpractice of using artificial colours, harmful chemicals, non-
edible oils etc. on vegetables and fruits and also create awareness among 
the vendors about ill effects of such practices. Recently, the Food 
Safety and Standards Authority of India, an autonomous statutory body 
under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, has been set up by the 
Government to look into all the matters related to Food Safety.

Production of wheat 
*91. SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that production of wheat is sufficient to 
meet the requirement of wheat eaters; 
(b) if not, whether steps are being taken to ensure enhanced 
production; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the expenditure incurred/likely to 
be incurred thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. 
Currently the production of wheat is sufficient to meet the domestic 
demand. However, to cope up with the expected increase in demand during 
the 11th Plan Period, it has been targeted to enhance production of wheat 
to 83.61 million tonnes by 2012 through the National Food Security 
Mission. For the period 2007-08 to 2011-12, an outlay of Rs.1920.33 crore 
has been provided for increasing wheat production through the Mission.

provided with 3898 RPF staff for access control duty.

Population Control 
*96. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of  HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the population in the country is increasing rapidly and it 
is expected to surpass the population of China; 
(b) if so, whether in view of steep rise in population, the Union 
Government proposes to have a fresh look at our Population Policy; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether the Union Government proposes to discuss the issue with 
the State Governments/UTs to effectively implement the Population Policy; 
and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) 
to (e) At the current rate, India's population is expected to exceed that 
of China before 2030 to become the most populous country in the World. 
India adopted a comprehensive and holistic National Population Policy 
(NPP), 2000, with clearly articulated objectives, strategic themes and 
operational strategies to meet the reproductive and child health needs of 
the people and to achieve net replacement level i.e. Total Fertility Rate 
(TFR) of 2.1 by 2010. It is based upon the need to simultaneously address 
issues of child survival, maternal health and contraception while 
increasing outreach and coverage of a comprehensive package of 
reproductive and child health services with G overnment, industry and the 
voluntary non-Government sector, working in partnership. TFR was 3.2 at 
the time when NPP 2000 was adopted and has declined to 2.7 as per Sample 
Registration Survey (SRS) 2007 conducted by Registrar General of India. 9 
States/UTs out of 20 major S tates as per size of population viz., Andhra 
Pradesh, Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Punjab, Karnataka, Maharashtra, 
Tamil Nadu, West Bengal have already achieved the replacement level TFR 
of 2.1. 5 States namely Assam, Gujarat, J&K, Haryana, Orissa, are hopeful 
of achieving the replacement level in the near future as they have 
attained TFR between 2.3 to 2.7. Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya 
Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, may not be able to achieve the 
replacement level by 2010 as these States have TFR from 3.1 to 3.9 as per 
SRS 2007.State wise level of TFR in 2000 and current level i.e. 2007 for 
major States is given in the Statement (See below). 
Government review the issue on Population Stabilization at different 
fora from time to time with the States/UTs. Regular visits are made by 

70 
Officers from the Government of India to understand the local issues of 
respective States and get them properly addressed at appropriate 
platform. The Government has launched the National Rural Health Mission 
on 12th April, 2005, throughout the country. Under the National Rural 
Health Mission (NRHM), emphasis has been laid to provide accessible, 
affordable, accountable, effective, reliable, and quality primary health 
care through creation of a cadre of Accredited Social Health Activities 
(ASHA), improved hospital care, decentralization of programme to district 
level to improve intra and inter- sectoral convergence and effective 
utilization of resources. 

71 
Population Stabilization is one of the objectives of NRHM. It provides 
a thrust for reduction of child and maternal mortality and reduces the 
fertility rates. The approach to population stabilization is to provide 
quality health services in remote rural areas along with a wide range of 
contraceptive choices to meet the unmet demands for these services. 
Efforts are on to provide quality Reproductive Health Services (including 
delivery, safe abortions, treatment of Reproductive tract infections and 
Family Planning Services to meet unmet needs, while ensuring full 
reproductive choices to women). The strategy also is to promote male 
participation in Family Planning. Population stabilization and Infant 
Mortality rate requires greater convergent action to influence the wider 
determinants of health care like female literacy, sanitation, nutrition, 
gender and social empowerment, early childhood development, marriage 
after 18, spacing of children and behavioural changes etc. Government is 
promoting IUD 380 intensively as a spacing method because of its 
longevity of 10 years and advantages over other IUDs. Fixed day fixed 
place Family Planning services round the year have been made possible on 
account of growing number of 24x7 PHCs and better functioning of CHCs and 
other health facilities, under NRHM. NRHM has increased the basket of 
choice by systematically and carefully introducing new and effective 
contraceptives in the programme. 
The Government has also launched a Family Planning (indemnity) 
Insurance Scheme since November, 2005, to provide insurance cover to 
acceptors of sterilization across the country. It also provides indemnity 
insurance cover to doctors/health facilities including private accredited 
facilities, as an effort towards encouraging adoption of sterilisation by 
eligible couples and giving protection to the service providers. The 
enhanced package of compensation for loss of wages to persons who undergo 
sterilization has been introduced since September 2007, resulting into 
increase in sterilisation during last one year.

*100. SHRIMATI RENUBALA PRADHAN: 
 SHRI B. J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government of Orissa had submitted a memorandum to the 
Union Government to provide market intelligence to the farmers to help 

80 
them to get remunerative prices for their agricultural produce especially 
in the tribal dominated Kandhamal district of the State; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, alongwith the status of the proposal; 
(c) whether a demand has also been made for setting up an Indian 
Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) unit in the region to study and 
solve the problems now being faced by the farmers; and 

81 
(d) if so, the details thereof along with status of the proposed? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (d) The 
suggestions in the Memorandum submitted by Government of Orissa included 
setting up of a research station by Indian Council of Agriculture 
Research (ICAR) in Kandhamal district of Orissa to study the problem of 
quality of the spices grown in the district and setting up a branch of 
Spices Board to provide market intelligence to the farmers and to market 
the spices. 
In order to help farmers to get remunerative prices for their 
agricultural produce, Government of India announces in each season 
Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for major agricultural commodities like 
paddy, wheat, oilseeds etc. and organizes purchase operations through 
public and cooperative agencies. A Market Intervention Scheme is in 
operation to be implemented on the request of State/U.T Government for 
procurement of agriculture and horticulture commodities generally 
perishable in nature and not covered under MSP, to protect the farmers 
from making distress sales in the event of fall in prices below economic 
level/cost of production. 
In order to facilitate better price realization by the farmers through 
improved marketing opportunities, Government has taken a number of 
initiatives to implement market reforms in agriculture. 
The Spices Board collects and publishes the domestic and international 
prices of spices on a weekly basis. Suggestion to set up a branch office 
of Spices Board in Kandhamal district was not found feasible by the 
Board. 
As regards the suggestion to set up an ICAR research station in the 
district of Kandhamal, it was not found feasible by ICAR in view of the 
existing facilities available in Orissa for research on spices.

568. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased 
to state:

is quite alarming;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL

total outlay of National Food Security, Mission is Rs.4882.48 crore for

Introduction of SRI 
569. SHRI A. ELAVARASAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the new System of Rice Intensification (SRI) has been 
introduced in the country with the support of World Bank which sharply 
cuts the use of water by 32 per cent and yields 40 to 80 per cent high 
per hectare than conventional rice cultivation; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and fiscal support provided by the 
World Bank for this purpose; 

111 
(c) whether Government will propose to introduce SRI in all parts of 
the country to boost rice cultivation; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reason therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL 
BHURIA): (a) The System of Rice Intensification (SRI) technique has 
received considerable attention globally including India due to its 
potential for yield improvement and water saving. The main features of 
this system include transplanting of young seedlings singly in a square 
pattern with wide spacing; using more  of  organic  fertilizers;  and  
keeping  the  paddy  field moist with intermittent drying and wetting  

112 
during the vegetative growth of plants. SRI causes better plant growth 
and development and economizes upon the use of seed, irrigation water, 
labour, plant protection chemicals and fertilizers and hence increases 
the productivity of land, water capital and  labour significantly over 
conventional method of rice cultivation. 
(b) The System of Rice Intensification technique is promoted under 
World Bank assisted project Irrigated Agriculture Modernized Water Bodies 
Restoration and Management (IAMWARM) in Tamil Nadu. During 2007- 08, 912 
demonstrations at the cost of Rs. 36.48 lakhs were organized. In 2008-09, 
a sum of Rs. 122.04 lakhs was spent for conducting 2034 demonstrations. 
(c) to (e) The popularization and promotion of SRI through demonstrations 
at farmers' field is one of the important interventions of National Food 
Security Mission-Rice (NFSM-Rice) which is in operation since October, 
2007 in 136 districts of 14 States (Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, 
Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Orissa, Tamilnadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal) in the 
country. Besides, the similar intervention is also implemented in 
Integrated Cereal Development Programme in Rice Based Cropping System 
Area (ICDP-Rice) in non-NFSM districts and States under Macro- Management 
Programme.

Fertilizers policy 
578. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government has finalised fertilizer 
policy and investment for gas based fertilizer projects; 

126 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the rate of subsidy proposed to be given for these projects? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS 
(SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) and (b) The Government has already finalized 
and announced a policy for  
new  investments in urea sector on 4th September 2008. The New Investment 
Policy aims at revamp,  

127 
expansion, revival of existing urea units and setting up of Greenfield 
projects. The policy is expected to substantially bridge the gap in next 
five years between the consumption and domestic production subject to 
confirmed and adequate availability of gas at reasonable prices. The 
salient features of the new investment policy are as under:- 
1. The policy is based on Import Parity Price (IPP) benchmark with 
suitable floor and ceiling prices. 
2. Floor & Ceiling prices: The floor for urea price is be kept at USD 250 
per MT and the ceiling for urea price is fixed at USD 425 per MT. 
3. Revamp project : Any improvement in capacity of existing plants 
through investment upto Rs. 1000 crore, in the existing train of 
ammonia-urea production will be treated as revamp of existing units. 
The additional urea from the revamp of existing units will be 
recognized at 85% of Import Parity Price with the floor and ceiling 
price as indicated above. 
4. Expansion projects: Setting up of a new ammonia-urea plant (a separate 
new ammonia-urea train) in the premises of the existing fertilizer 
plants, utilizing some of the common utilities will qualify for being 
treated as expansion project. The investment should exceed a minimum 
limit of Rs.3000 crore. The urea from the expansion of existing units 
will be recognized at 90% of IPP, with the floor and ceiling price as 
indicated above. 
5. Revival/Brownfield projects: The urea from the revived units of 
Hindustan Fertilizer Corporation Limited (HFCL) and Fertilizer 
Corporation of India Limited (FCIL) will be recognized at 95% of IPP 
with prescribed floor & ceiling price, if the revival of closed units 
takes placed in public sector. 
6. Greenfield projects: The pricing of Greenfield projects will be 
decided based on a bidding process which will be for a discount over 
IPP, after firming up of the location (States) of the proposed new 
plants. 
7. Gas transportation charges: An additional gas transportation cost will 
be paid to units undertaking expansion and revival on the basis of 
actuals (upto 5.2 Gcal per MT of urea) as deci ded by the Regulator 
(Gas) subject to a maximum ceiling of USD 25 per MT of urea.  
8. Allocation of Gas: Only non- APM gas will be considered for the new 
investment in urea sector. 
9. Coal gasification based Urea Projects: The Coal gasification based 

128 
urea projects will also be treated on par with a revival or a 
Greenfield project as the case may be. In addition, any other 
incentives or tax benefits as provided by Government for encouraging 
coal gasification technology will also be extended to these projects. 
10. Joint Ventures abroad: The Joint Venture projects abroad in gas 
rich countries are also proposed to be encouraged through firm offtake 
contracts with pricing decided on the basis of prevailing market 
conditions and in mutual consultation with the joint venture company. 
However, the principle for deciding upon the maximum price will be the 
price achieved under Greenfield projects or 95% of IPP as proposed for 
revival projects (in absence of any Greenfield projects) with a cap of 
USD 405 CIF India per MT and a floor of USD 225 CIF India per MT 
(inclusive of handling and bagging costs). 

129 
11. Time period for proposed investment policy: Only those revamp 
projects which start production of additional capacities within four 
years of notification of the new policy would qualify for the 
dispensation recommended above. Similarly production from expansion 
and revival (brownfield) units that come about within five years of 
notification of the new policy would qualify for dispensation provided 
in the policy. If the production does not come through within the 
stipulated time period, such brownfield projects will be treated 
similar to a Greenfield projects wherein price will be decided through 
limited bidding options. The time period for setting up of new Joint 
Ventures would also be five years under the new investment policy. 
(c) Subsidy for urea produced from the new investments will be a 
function of the prevailing maximum retail price (MRP) and the pricing of 
urea as indicated in the salient features of the policy enumerated above.

Increase in drug prices by pharma companies 
†586. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware-  of the fact that the prices of 
certain drugs have been substantially increased by pharma companies; 
(b) whether Government would take any action against pharma companies 
which have increased the prices of drugs in protest against Government 
policy on curbing price rise; and 
(c) the measures to be taken by Government for procurement of cheaper 
drugs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS 
(SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) and (b) No such information has been brought to 
the notice of the Government/NPPA that the prices of certain drugs have 
been substantially increased by pharma companies. 
The 74 bulk drugs specified in the First Schedule of the Drugs (Prices 
Control) Order, 1995 (DPCO, 95) and the formulations based thereon are 
under price control and their prices are fixed / revised by the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) in accordance with the provisions 
of the DPCO, 95. The price fixation/revision of the Scheduled medicines 
is a continuous process under DPCO, 1995. 
Prices of non- Scheduled drugs are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the various factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc. The Government 
takes corrective measures where the public interest is found to be 
adversely affected. NPPA regularly monitors the prices and availability 
of the drugs in the country and wherever required, corrective action is 
taken in the matter. 
(c) Purchase of medicines by Government is made through tenders. These 
purchases are made in bulk which helps in getting quality drugs at 
competitive prices.

Adulteration of gold with iridium and ruthenium 
588. SHRI DHARAMPAL SABHARWAL: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware of the adulteration of gold with 
iridium; 
(b) if so, the complete details in this regard; 
(c) how many goldsmiths have been arrested in the country for 
adulterating the precious metal with iridium and ruthenium; and 
(d) the steps being taken against the guilties for adulterating gold, 
so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND 
PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) and (b) The Department of 
Commerce has received an anonymous complaint, inter- alia, alleging that 
jewellers mix iridium with gold. Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) is also 
aware that gold can be adulterated with iridium. Therefore, provision has 
been made in the relevant Indian Standard for Gold and Gold Alloys, 
Jewellery/Artifacts - fineness and marking, IS  1417:1999 that gold 
alloys for manufacturing jewellery/artifacts and gold solders shall be  
free from iridium. 
(c) and (d) The Scheme of Hallmarking of Gold Jewellery being operated 
by BIS is voluntary in nature at present. So, BIS ensures that gold 
jewellery of its licenced jewellers conform to the relevant Indian 
Standard. BIS has no statutory powers under the Bureau of Indian 
Standards Act, 1986 to take action against jewellers who are not BIS 
licensees and are involved in malpractices.

and review with State & UT Governments, Government has been getting 
functioning of TPDS evaluated from time to time through independent 
agencies. Since earlier evaluation studies conducted by PEO, Planning 
Commission and ORG MARG reported in 2005 that there were diversions and

being emphasized.

of BPL 'and AAY families at fair price shops, display of allocated 
quantities on web sites, adoption and implementation of revised 
Citizens Charter, monthly certification of delivery of foodgrains to 
fair price shops and their distribution to ration card holders and 
taking up publicity-cum-awareness campaign have been initiated. 
(iii) Improved vigilance at various levels and strict penal action 
against those involved in malpractices, including action against staff 
responsible for issuing ineligible ration cards and persons found in 
possession of such ration cards are being emphasized. 
(iv) Introduction of new technologies such as Computerization of TPDS 
operations at various levels, smart- card-based delivery of essential 
commodities, use of global positioning system on vehicles transporting 
TPDS commodities and bar coding of ration cards, etc., is being 
piloted. 
With these measures, functioning of TPDS is getting streamlined. To 
assess impact of all these initiatives, concurrent evaluation of TPDS has 
been taken up in 26 States & UTs.

Public Distribution System  

161 
(TPDS) is operated under the joint responsibility of the Central and the 
State/UT Governments. The Central Government has taken the responsibility 
for procurement, storage, transportation and bulk allocation of 
foodgrains to the States and UTs. The operational responsibilities far 
allocation of foodgrains within the States/UTs, identification of

Government got functioning of TPDS evaluated by Programme Evaluation

To assess impact of implementation of 9- point action plan, Government 
has undertaken concurrent evaluation of TPDS in 26 States and UTs where 
earlier studies bad indicated malpractices. National Council of Applied 
Economic Research (NCAER) has completed this study m 12 States. First 
report of NCAER received in November 2007 for Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, 
Mizoram, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh contains an estimation of number of 
families in the country in 2006. Based on it, NCAER has drawn an 
inference about 2.3 crore ration cards in the tountry being in excess of 
that estimate. However, this inferred number is of excess ration cards 
and not of bogus ration cards. Similarly, the study report mentions its 
estimate of unidentified families, that is those without having ration 
cards at 1.2 crore at the All India Level. Based on these calculations, 
the report has mentioned identification errors as inclusion of non poor 
and exclusion of poor from food subsidy. 
Since the State/UT Governments are responsible for proper 
identification of BPL and AAY families under TPDS and issuance of ration 
cards to them, copy of the NCAER report has been sent to the concerned 
State Governments for taking required action.

the rural areas of the country, especially for poor women and children,

Acid tablets during pregnancy and lactation; Organizing Village Health & 
Nutrition Day at Anganwadi Centers; Appointment of an Accredited Social

the community including pregnant women; Strengthening of Health 
Facilities, that is, District Hospitals, Community health Centres (CHCs),

with funds including untied grants, Annual Maintenance Grants (AMG) and

 DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI:

(SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) Yes, The National Rural Health 
Mission (NRHM) is an overarching umbrella initiative for establishing a 
functional, community owned, decentralized health delivery system with 
inter sector convergence at all levels. 
The Government undertakes periodic reviews of National Rural H ealth 
Mission (NRHM). These reviews are part of the detailed self contained 
multifaceted monitoring framework built within NRHM. The progress of NRHM 
is also reviewed as part of the process of approval of Annual Programme 
Implementation Plans (PIP) of the States which is currently underway. 
The 2nd Common Review Mission of NRHM has recently been completed. The 
Review Mission is a detailed month long process involving desk analysis 
as well as field visits to selected S tates. During the 2nd CRM, thirteen 
representative States were; covered and findings have been compiled into 
reports which were shared with S tate Governments concerned for remedial 
action. The dissemination of the findings as well as remedial actions 
proposed by the S tates has been recently conducted at a National level 
workshop. The CRM has provided critical insights into innovations being 
undertaken in the S tates and bottlenecks of Human Resources, 
Infrastructure, procurement and supply etc. being faced by them. The 
Government is assisting the S tates with additional funding as well as 
technical inputs to overcome these bottlenecks. The experience sharing 
amongst States which takes place during the periodic reviews has allowed 
States to take up innovative, S tate specific solutions to the 
deficiencies.

(NRHM) launched in 2005 is seeking to address the inadequacies in health 
infrastructure through provision of funds to public health as per the 
norms enlisted in Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS). The State/UTs 
Governments reflect their priorities for upgradation of health services 
in their annual Programme Implementation Plan under NRHM. Funds are 
released to State/UT Governments as per the approval of National 
Programme Coordination Committee (NPCC) under NRHM.

of the country are as under: 
• To achieve an acceptable standard of good health amongst the general 
Population of the country. 
• Increased access to the decentralized public health system by 
establishing new infrastructure in deficient area and by upgrading the 
infrastructure in the existing institutions. 
• To ensure more equitable access to health service across the social 
and geographical expanse of the country. 
• Emphasis will be given to increasing the aggregate public health 
investment through a substantially increased contribution by Central 
Government. 
• The contribution of private sector in providing health services would 
be much enhanced, particularly for the population which can afford to 
pay for services. 
• Primacy will be given to preventive and first line curative 
initiatives at primary health level through increased sectoral share 
of allocation. 
• Emphasis will be laid on rational use of drugs within the allopathic 
system.

will be ensured.

the rural areas of the country, especially for poor women and children,
